Which of the following represents the pulmonary circulation?
  1. A. The left heart and systemic arteries, capillaries, and veins
  2. B. The left heart and pulmonary arteries, capillaries, and veins
  3. C. The right heart and systemic arteries, capillaries, and veins
  4. D. The right heart and pulmonary arteries, capillaries, and veins
AnswerD. The right heart and pulmonary arteries, capillaries, and veins
WhyThe pulmonary circulation starts at the right ventricle, which pumps blood through the pulmonary arteries, capillaries and veins back to the left atrium.
ConceptPulmonary circulation = right heart + pulmonary arteries, capillaries, veins

8
In which of the following situations is pulmonary blood flow greater than aortic blood flow?
  1. A. Normal adult
  2. B. Fetus
  3. C. Left-to-right ventricular shunt
  4. D. Right-to-left ventricular shunt
  5. E. Right ventricular failure
  6. F. Administration of a positive inotropic agent
AnswerC. Left-to-right ventricular shunt
WhyIn a left-to-right shunt, part of the LV output passes through the septal defect into the right ventricle, so right ventricular (pulmonary) flow exceeds left ventricular (aortic) flow.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C [I A]. In a left-to-right ventricular shunt, a defect in the ventricular septum allows blood to flow from the left ventricle to the right ventricle instead of being ejected into the aorta. The “shunted” fraction of the left ventricular output is therefore added to the output of the right ventricle, making pulmonary blood flow (the cardiac output of the right ventricle) higher than systemic blood flow (the cardiac output of the left ventricle). In normal adults, the outputs of both ventricles are equal in the steady state. In the fetus, pulmonary blood flow is near zero. Right ventricular failure results in decreased pulmonary blood flow. Administration of a positive inotropic agent should have the same effect on contractility and cardiac output in both ventricles.
ConceptLeft-to-right shunt → pulmonary blood flow exceeds aortic blood flow
9
Compared with the systemic circulation, the pulmonary circulation has a
  1. A. higher blood flow
  2. B. lower resistance
  3. C. higher arterial pressure
  4. D. higher capillary pressure
  5. E. higher cardiac output
AnswerB. lower resistance
WhyBoth circuits carry the whole cardiac output, but pulmonary pressures are far lower, so by R = ΔP/Q pulmonary vascular resistance is about one-tenth of TPR.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B [VI A]. Blood flow (or cardiac output) in the systemic and pulmonary circulations is nearly equal; pulmonary flow is slightly less than systemic flow because about 2% of the systemic cardiac output bypasses the lungs. The pulmonary circulation is characterized by both lower pressure and lower resistance than the systemic circulation, so flows through the two circulations are approximately equal (flow = pressure/resistance).
ConceptPulmonary vs systemic circulation: same flow, lower resistance (and pressure)

A 64-year-old woman with acute myocardial infarction develops a rupture of her papillary muscle anchoring the chordae tendineae of the mitral valve. She becomes short of breath with rales (crackles) on the lung exam. What is the mechanism of the lung finding?
  1. A. Increased right atrial pressure
  2. B. Increased left atrial and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
  3. C. Increased compliance of lungs
  4. D. Decreased elasticity of lungs
  5. E. Shunt circulation
AnswerB. Increased left atrial and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
WhyA ruptured papillary muscle lets the mitral valve leak, so blood regurgitates into the left atrium, raising left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressure and pushing fluid into the lungs.
Explanation from the source
Bicuspid cannot close → blood regurgitates back in left atrium increasing pressure therefore increasing pulmonary capillary pressure as blood is backed up towards lungs → cause pulmonary edema | slide 38: Ruptured papillary muscles makes it harder to open mitral valve – causes backpressure
ConceptPapillary muscle rupture → mitral regurgitation → ↑ LA and pulmonary capillary pressure → rales

During the cardiac cycle, blood is ejected from the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery. Which of the following events occurs simultaneously with this ejection phase in the left side of the heart?
  1. A. Blood fills the left ventricle as the mitral valve is open
  2. B. The left ventricle contracts and blood is ejected into the aorta
  3. C. Blood flows from the left atrium to the left ventricle as the aortic valve opens
  4. D. The left atrium contracts, pushing blood through the mitral valve into the left ventricle
AnswerB. The left ventricle contracts and blood is ejected into the aorta
WhyBoth ventricles are activated together through the bundle branches, so ventricular systole is simultaneous: while the RV ejects into the pulmonary artery, the LV ejects into the aorta.
Explanation from the source
The right and left ventricles contract simultaneously during systole, which means that while the right ventricle is ejecting blood into the pulmonary artery, the left ventricle is ejecting blood into the aorta.
ConceptRight and left ventricles eject at the same time (RV ejection = LV ejection into aorta)

  1. A. Vena cava > Left atrium > Tricuspid valve > Left Ventricle > Pulmonic valve > Pulmonary artery > Lungs > Pulmonary vein > Right atrium > Mitral valve > Right ventricle > Aortic valve > Aorta
  2. B. Vena cava > Right atrium > Tricuspid valve > Right Ventricle > Pulmonic valve > Pulmonary artery > Lungs > Pulmonary vein > Left atrium > Mitral valve > Left ventricle > Aortic valve > Aorta

During strenuous exercise, the percentage of cardiac output to skeletal and cardiac muscle increases. Which of the following mechanisms accomplishes this?
  1. A. Blood flow is redistributed among organ systems by altering arteriolar resistance, increasing flow to skeletal and cardiac muscle at expense of other organs.
  2. B. The compliance of the vessels towards cardiac and skeletal muscle increase, increasing their ability to hold larger volumes at lower pressures, increasing flow.
  3. C. Cardiac output increases, while the percentages of flow to each organ remains the same.
  4. D. A & B
  5. E. A & C
AnswerA. Blood flow is redistributed among organ systems by altering arteriolar resistance, increasing flow to skeletal and cardiac muscle at expense of other organs.
Key changed: The source key was E (A & C). Option C says each organ's percentage stays the same, which contradicts the stem; only A raises the muscle and heart share.
WhyCardiac output is divided among parallel organ beds by their arteriolar resistance, so metabolic dilation in muscle and heart plus sympathetic constriction elsewhere redistributes flow toward working muscle.
Explanation from the source
an increase in compliance would make a vessel able to hold larger volumes at lower pressures, but this is not what happens during exercise and would have no effect on flow. Page 119 in Costanzo
ConceptMechanism that raises the share of CO to skeletal and cardiac muscle in exercise

64. Y.o male with 20 year smoking history presenting to his physician complaining of shortness of breath, exercise intolerance and fatigue. Upon examination, pt is positive for pulmonary edema ,and fine crackles are heard at the bases. No peripheral edema is noted. Pt is subsequently diagnosed with heart failure. Which side of the heart do you suspect is failing?
  1. a. Right side
  2. b. Left side
Answerb. Left side
WhyA failing left ventricle backs blood up into the left atrium and pulmonary veins, raising pulmonary capillary pressure and causing pulmonary edema; peripheral edema would point to right-sided failure.
Explanation from the source
As the left side of the heart is failing, it can no longer pump blood out to the systemic circulation efficiently. Blood start backing up into the pulmonary circulation. This in turn increases pulmonary vein pressure. This increase in pressure forces the fluids out of the circulation into the lung tissue, resulting in pulmonary edema. Notice the pt does not have peripheral edema, which would indicate a R sided heart failure as the fluid will back up into the systemic circulation. (off note- in progression of L sided heart failure, and increase in pulmonary pressure, R sided heart failure can develop as well).
ConceptPulmonary edema without peripheral edema → left-sided heart failure

Which one of the following characteristics is most similar in the systemic and pulmonary circulations?
  1. A. Stroke work
  2. B. Preload
  3. C. Afterload
  4. D. Peak systolic pressure
  5. E. Blood volume
AnswerB. Preload
WhyThe two ventricles are in series and eject the same stroke volume, so their end-diastolic volumes (preload) are nearly equal, while afterload, stroke work and systolic pressure are far higher on the left.
Explanation from the source
The answer is b. (Rhoades, pp 372-376.) The right and left ventriPeak systolic pressure cles are in series with one another so that the entire cardiac output (except for a small anatomic shunt) passes through both circulations. Since the two Blood volume ventricles beat at the same rate, their stroke volumes are the same. However, the resistance of the pulmonary vasculature is much smaller than that of the systemic circulation; thus, the afterload and stroke work are greater on the left side than on the right side. Because the same cardiac output is ejected into a higher resistance, peak systolic pressure is higher on the left side than on the right side. Only about 10% of the blood volume is within the pulmonary circulation at any one time. About two-thirds of the blood volume is stored within the systemic veins and venules. Although the left and right preloads are not identical, they are very similar.
ConceptSystemic vs pulmonary circulation: preload is the most similar characteristic

The greatest percentage of blood volume is found in the
  1. A. Heart
  2. B. Aorta
  3. C. Distributing arteries and arterioles
  4. D. Capillaries
  5. E. Venules and veins
AnswerE. Venules and veins
WhyThe thin-walled, highly compliant venules and veins act as the blood reservoir, holding about 60–65% of total blood volume.
Explanation from the source
The answer is e. (Guyton, p 160.) The total circulating blood volume is approximately 70 mL/kg, about two-thirds of which is found in the systemic veins and venules. A significant volume of blood (15%) is found. in the pulmonary circulation. The large volume of blood found on the venous side of the circulation is used to adjust circulating blood volume. For example during hemorrhage, contraction of the veins and venules of the skin increases the amount of blood available for perfusion of the heart and brain.
ConceptGreatest blood volume resides in the veins (venules and veins)

Which site has the greatest control over systemic blood pressure?

  2. B.Venules
  3. C.Arterioles
  4. D.Arteries
  5. E.Capillaries
AnswerC. Arterioles

A patient who is hypotensive, obtunded, and tachycardic due to a recent infection that has caused sepsis. Norepinephrine (alpha-1 agonist) is administered to bring up the BP. What is the effect of pressors on the systemic vasculature?
  1. A.Resistance will increase proportionally to the decrease in radius
  2. B.Resistance will decrease by a factor of 2 due to the decrease in radius
  3. C.Resistance will increase by a factor of 4 due to the decrease in radius
  4. D.Resistance will increase by a factor of 2 due to the decrease in radius
  5. E.Resistance will decrease proportionally due to the decrease in radius

Whyα1 vasoconstriction narrows arterioles, and by Poiseuille resistance varies with 1/r⁴, so it rises with the fourth power of the fall in radius, the "factor of 4" in this key (halving r gives 2⁴ = 16-fold).
Conceptα1 agonist (norepinephrine) ↓ arteriolar radius → ↑ resistance (r⁴ dependence)

A woman has her renal blood flow measured by a flow meter, and the flow is found to be 400 mL/min. Pressure probes are placed in her left renal artery and left renal vein. Renal arterial pressure is found to be 120 mmHg, and renal venous pressure is found to be 20 mmHg. What is the vascular resistance of the left kidney in this woman?
  1. A. 0.30 mmHg / mL per min
  2. B. 0.35 mmHg / mL per min
  3. C. 0.18 mmHg / mL per min
  4. D. 0.20 mmHg / mL per min
  5. E. 0.25 mmHg / mL per min
AnswerE. 0.25 mmHg / mL per min
WhyRenal vascular resistance R = ΔP/Q = (120 − 20 mm Hg)/400 mL/min = 0.25 mm Hg/mL per min.
Explanation from the source
● Resistance can be found by using the equation for blood flow: Q = ∆P / R ● Rearranging for R, we can solve for resistance: R = ∆P / Q ● ∆P = Pressure in renal artery - Pressure in renal vein (120 mmHg - 20 mmHg) ● Q = Renal blood flow = 400 mL per min ● R = (120 mmHg - 20 mmHg) / 400 mL per min = 0.25 mmHg / mL per min This question is a modified version of the sample problem found on page 123 of Costanzo physiology.
ConceptCalculate vascular resistance R = ΔP / Q (renal artery − vein, flow)

A 77-year-old man presents to ED with unilateral weakness, vision changes, and slurred speech. He is found to have suffered a stroke due to partial occlusion of his right internal carotid artery. An MRI of the right internal carotid artery shows a 75% occlusion. Assuming that blood flow through the right internal was 500 mL/min prior to the occlusion, what is blood flow through the artery after the occlusion?
  1. A. 250 mL/min
  2. B. 1.95 mL/min
  3. C. 375 mL/min
  4. D. 1.56 mL/min
  5. E. 125 mL/min
AnswerB. 1.95 mL/min
WhyA 75% occlusion leaves ¼ of the radius, and flow varies with r⁴ (Poiseuille), so flow falls to (¼)⁴ = 1/256: 500/256 ≈ 1.95 mL/min.
Explanation from the source
● Use Poiseullie’s Equation! ● A 75% occlusion means a 75% decrease in the radius AKA ¼ the radius ● Plugging in (¼) for r in Poiseullie’s Equation means a 256-fold increase in resistance (R), since radius is to the 4th power ● If we plug this into the equation for blood flow (Q = ∆P / R), then we get a 256-fold decrease in flow ● A 256-fold decrease is the same as saying 1/256, or 0.0039 (or 0.39%) ● If pre-occlusion flow was 500 mL/min, then the post-occlusion flow is 0.39% of that ● 0.39% of 500 mL/min is 1.95 mL/min This question is a modified version of the sample problem found on page 124 of Costanzo physiology.
Concept75% occlusion (r → ¼) → flow ↓ 256-fold by r⁴: 500 → 1.95 mL/min

The presence of a dicrotic notch in systolic pressure signifies an abnormality (This is normal, brief retrograde flow of blood) E. The difference between the systolic and diastolic pressure is the mean arterial pressure. (This is the formula for the pulse pressure)

  4. D. Laminar flow increases

92
Each of the following slides are titled with different cardiovascular conditions. Please draw (superimposed on normal loop) the loop you are likely to observe with the indicated condition. You can presume that the condition has not yet led to marked remodeling of the left ventricle. Acute Aortic Stenosis
AnswerLeft ventricular emptying is impaired because of high outflow resistance caused by a reduction in the valve orifice area High outflow resistance causes a large pressure gradient across the aortic valve during ejection, such that the peak systolic pressure increases This leads to an increase in ventricular afterload, a decrease in stroke volume, and an increase in end-systolic volume. An increased in end-systolic volume leads an increase in venous return which then leads to an increase in end-diastolic volume and preload
WhyAcute aortic stenosis raises outflow resistance, so the LV must build a much higher peak systolic pressure to eject; SV falls and ESV rises, and the leftover volume slightly raises EDV.
Explanation from the source
What condition is this? Aortic valve stenosis What does it cause? Marked increase in LV pressure during systole and large increase in aortic pulse pressure What happens to P-V loop as a result? LVEDV: a stenotic aortic valve will impair outflow from LV to aorta. As a result, there will be increased ESV. The increased ESV will ultimately lead to a slightly increased EDV. LVESV: a stenotic aortic valve will impair outflow from the LV to the aorta. That means that the aortic valve will “open” at a higher pressure and “close” at a higher pressure. The result is that SV will be markedly reduced and the LV systolic pressure will be greatly increased to overcome the additional afterload imparted by the stenotic aortic valve. Stroke volume: see LVESV. Will be greatly reduced. Cardiac output: cardiac output is HRxSV. If stroke volume is decreased, will HR “pick up the slack”? Yes, but it cannot pick up all of the slack. As a result, CO will be lower. Systolic aortic pressure: EDV is up (should increase contractility [Frank Starling], left ventricular systolic pressure is way up…BUT cardiac output will be lower due to the stenotic valve, thus, you’d expect to see a significant decrease in systolic aortic pressure.
ConceptPV loop, acute aortic stenosis: ↑ peak systolic pressure, ↓ SV, ↑ ESV/EDV
Slides
93
Each of the following slides are titled with different cardiovascular conditions. Please draw (superimposed on normal loop) the loop you are likely to observe with the indicated condition. You can presume that the condition has not yet led to marked remodeling of the left ventricle. Acute Aortic Regurgitation
AnswerAortic valve does not completely close @ the end of systolic ejection  blood flows back into the LV during diastole Enhanced ventricular filling causes an increase in end-diastolic volume The increased EDV activates the Frank-Starling mechanism to increase force of contraction, ventricular peak systolic pressure, and stroke volume
WhyIn acute aortic regurgitation blood leaks back from the aorta into the LV during diastole, so EDV rises and, by Frank–Starling, force, peak systolic pressure and total stroke volume increase.
Explanation from the source
What condition is this? Aortic valve regurgitation/insufficiency What does it cause? Backflow of blood into left ventricle during ventricular diastole. What happens to P-V loop as a result? LVEDV: regurgitation at the aortic valve will allow blood from the aorta to “leak” into the left ventricle. This will augment ventricular filling from the atria and increase LVEDV. LVESV: Isovolumic relaxation is affected by aortic insufficiency. Thus, blood is allowed to leak into the LV during this time which ultimately results in an increased LVESV. Cardiac output: cardiac output is HRxSV. Here, stroke volume is increased (increased EDV, contractility and even reduced afterload [“loose” valve]…. as a compensatory mechanism. HOWEVER, forward cardiac output is decreased as we get “leak” backwards. Systolic aortic pressure: Increased EDV, contraction, and SV all contribute to a increased systolic aortic pressure.
ConceptPV loop, acute aortic regurgitation: ↑ EDV, ↑ SV, ↑ peak systolic pressure

After chugging a few Alanis, Physiology Lead TA Maram experiences an increase in blood pressure associated with caffeine-induced vasoconstriction. The radius of one of her arterioles decreases by ½. Assuming the pressure gradient, blood viscosity, and vessel length remain constant, which of the following best describes the resulting changes in vascular resistances, blood flow, and Reynold’s number? [table columns: Vascular Resistance | Blood Flow | Reynolds Number]
Show figure
  1. A. 4-fold increase | 4-fold decrease | 2-fold increase
  2. B. 16 fold increase | 16 fold decrease | 8 fold increase
  3. C. 16 fold increase | 16 fold decrease | 8 fold decrease
  4. D. 16 fold decrease | 16 fold increase | 8 fold increase
  5. E. 8 fold increase | 8 fold decrease | 4 fold decrease
AnswerC. 16 fold increase | 16 fold decrease | 8 fold decrease
WhyHalving r raises resistance 2⁴ = 16-fold, so flow (Q = ΔP/R) falls 16-fold; velocity = Q/A = (1/16)/(1/4) = ¼, so Reynolds number (∝ d × v) = ½ × ¼ = ⅛, an 8-fold decrease.
Explanation from the source
Using Poiseuille’s Law: Resistance is proportional to 1/r4 = 1/(½)4 = 1/(1/16) = 16 fold increase in resistance Using Q= (ΔP)/R, with a constant pressure, Q = 1/16, or a 16-fold decrease in flow Using v=Q/A → (1/16)/(¼) = ¼ or a 4-fold decrease in velocity. Since the radius decreased by ½, the diameter also decreased by ½. Plugging into Reynold’s equation, we get an 8-fold decrease
ConceptRadius halved (fixed ΔP): R ↑16×, flow ↓16×, Reynolds number ↓8×

At any given moment, most of your blood is in your venous system. Capacitance can be thought of as the ability to hold volume without a drastic change in pressure. Hence veins have the highest capacitance because of their elastic nature and distensibility and thus hold the greatest amounts of blood volume.

WhySystolic pressure is the peak arterial pressure during ejection, so it exceeds MAP and diastolic pressure, and pulse pressure is only their difference (120 − 80 = 40).
Explanation from the source
Systolic pressure: pressure in your arteries when your heart beats, and is always the higher number in a blood pressure reading. Diastolic pressure: Pressure in your arteries when your heart relaxes between beats, and is the lower number in a blood pressure reading Pulse Pressure: systolic – diastolic (e.g 120-80 =40) Mean arterial pressure: ave pressure in arteries during a single cardiac cycle (normal = 70-100mmHg)
ConceptSystolic pressure is the highest of SP, DP, PP and MAP

Which of the following statements about resistance in a blood vessel is correct?
  1. A. Resistance is increased as the compliance of the blood vessel is increased
  2. B. Resistance is increased as the diameter of the blood vessel is increased
  3. C. Resistance is increased as the length of the blood vessel is increased
  4. D. Resistance is increased as the viscosity of the blood is decreased
AnswerC. Resistance is increased as the length of the blood vessel is increased
WhyBy Poiseuille, R = 8ηl/πr⁴, so resistance rises in direct proportion to vessel length (and viscosity) and falls with the fourth power of radius.
Explanation from the source
Longer vessel provides a greater surface area for friction between the blood and the vessel walls, which impedes the blood's flow. A longer blood vessel creates more resistance and consequently lowers blood flow

An 80-year-old man had problems with his AV conduction system, and his cardiologist decided that an artificial pacemaker was required. Some of the results were as follows: When the heart was paced at 60 beats/min, the patient’s stroke volume was 80 ml, his cardiac output was 4.8 L/min, and his total peripheral resistance was 20 mm Hg/L/min. When the heart was paced at 100 beats/min, the stroke volume was 48 ml, his cardiac output was 4.8 L/min, and his total peripheral resistance was 20 mm Hg/L/min. 2. What directional changes in the arterial systolic, diastolic, and pulse pressure would you expect when the paced heart was switched from 60 to 100 beats/min?
Answera. With a lower stroke volume, you would expect systolic pressure to be decreased (less volume in aorta w/ each beat). However, diastolic pressure is actually slightly higher (less diastolic time with decreased time between ventricular contractions). Remember, mean arterial pressure was the same. With a lower systolic and higher diastolic pressure, the pulse pressure is lower (SBP-DBP).
WhyAt 100/min each beat ejects less (48 vs 80 mL), so systolic falls, and the shorter diastole leaves less runoff time, so diastolic rises; pulse pressure narrows while MAP stays 96 mm Hg.
ConceptPacing 60→100 bpm at same CO: ↓ systolic, slight ↑ diastolic, ↓ pulse pressure

2. Jenny goes to the doctor's office and finds out that the pressure of her right renal artery is 150 mmHg and her right renal venous pressure is 60 mmHg. She also finds out that her renal blood flow is measured at 250 ml/min. What is Jenny's right kidney's vascular resistance?
Show figure
  1. a. 0.36 mL per min/ mmHg

  3. c. 0.41 mL per min/ mmHg
  4. d. 0.36 mmHg/ mL per min

The following diagram illustrates the relative resistance of three vessels. The ratio of the flow in vessel X to the flow in vessel Z is:
  1. a) 3:4
  2. b) 4:3
  3. c) 4:1
  4. d) 1:1
  5. e) 3:2
Answerb) 4:3
WhyVessel X carries the total flow, which splits between parallel Y (R = 9) and Z (R = 3) in inverse proportion to resistance, so Z takes 3/4 of it and X : Z = 4 : 3.
Explanation from the source
Major takeaway here is that the flow going through X = flow of Y + flow of Z. The proportion of fluid that travels through Y and Z is inversely proportional to their resistance. Remember, if one of the vessels had infinite resistance, nothing would flow through it! Let’s call flow Q and resistance R. Qy/Qz = Rz/Ry = 9/3. So 3x as much fluid flows through Z as does Y. In other words, for every 1L of fluid that travels through Y, 3L will travel through Z. In other words, if we have 4L of fluid go through X, 1L will go through Y and 3L will go through Z. So our ratio of QX to QZ is 4:3!
ConceptSeries–parallel vessels: flow ratio of vessel X to vessel Z (figure)

Thanks to Touro, you’re very stressed, and your blood pressure is high. To relieve this, you take a medication that targets the vessels located directly before the capillary bed. What best describes the mechanism of action of your drug and the receptor it acts on?
  1. A. Increases IP3/Ca2+; commonly found in skeletal muscle
  2. B. Decreases IP3/Ca2+; commonly found in skeletal muscle
  3. C. Increases IP3/Ca2+; commonly found in skin and splanchnic vasculature
  4. D. Decreases IP3/Ca2+; commonly found in skin and splanchnic vasculature
  5. E. Increases cAMP; commonly found in skin and splanchnic vasculature
  6. F. Decreases cAMP; commonly found in skin and splanchnic vasculature
AnswerD. Decreases IP3/Ca2+; commonly found in skin and splanchnic vasculature
WhyArteriolar α1 receptors (Gq → IP3/Ca²⁺) dominate in skin and splanchnic beds, so an α1 blocker lowers IP3/Ca²⁺, relaxing arterioles and reducing TPR and BP.
Explanation from the source
You are taking an alpha-1 blocker, which dilates the arterioles of the skin and splanchnic muscle by antagonizing the Gq receptor. Contrast this with beta-2, which is found in skeletal muscle and works through the Gs pathway. See speaker notes for more! Many blood pressure medications tend to work by antagonizing the alpha-1 receptor. Why? Because the majority of resistance in circulation occurs in the arterioles, which are primarily innervated by alpha-1 receptors. If we block these receptors, we get the most change in blood pressure.
ConceptArteriolar antihypertensive: α1 blockade ↓ IP3/Ca²⁺; α1 in skin/splanchnic beds

A patient who takes prazosin (alpha-1 receptor antagonist) accidentally took an extra dose of their medication and is feeling lightheaded. Which of the following accurately describes this reaction?

  2. B. Decreased Gq activity causes increased elasticity in large arteries
  3. C. Decreased Gq activity causes increased compliance in veins

When metabolic production is low (e.g., nonexercising muscle), the sympathetic tone controls the amount of blood flowing into the organ. The precapillary sphincters control the distribution of blood within an organ, supplying blood to cells that are more active and restricting blood flow to those that are less active. The arteries, postcapillary venules, and veins are not involved in regulation of blood flow through individual organs.
ConceptArteriolar resistance regulates distribution of blood among organs

Match each letter with its phase and corresponding ion movement
AnswerA) Phase 4- Potassium efflux and Na+ and Ca2+ influx keeps the cell at negative resting potential B) Phase 0- Na influx C) Phase 1- Na channels close, K channels open D) Phase 2- Ca channels open and counter the action at the K channels E) Phase 3- Ca channels close and K channels remain open
Sources disagree on the key:
  • Canvas 2026 › Medical Physiology I › Physiology I Exam 2 TA Review-1.pdf · 57: A) Phase 4- Potassium efflux and Na+ and Ca2+ influx keeps the cell at negative resting potential B) Phase 0- Na influx C) Phase 1- Na channels close, K channels open D) Phase 2- Ca channels open and counter the action at the K channels E) Phase 3- Ca channels close and K channels remain open
  • Canvas 2026 › Medical Physiology I › Physiology I Exam 2 TA Review-1.pdf · 63: A) Phase 4- Funny Na+ channels open B) Phase 0- Influx of Ca2+ C) Phase 3- Efflux of K+
  • SGA Drive › Physiology Middletown + Harlem (Previous Years) › Physio Exam 2 › Physio Exam 2 › Physiology I Exam 2 TA Review.pptx · 57: A) Phase 4- Potassium efflux and Na+ and Ca2+ influx keeps the cell at negative resting potential B) Phase 0- Na influx C) Phase 1- Na channels close, K channels open D) Phase 2- Ca channels open and counter the action at the K channels E) Phase 3- Ca channels close and K channels remain open
  • SGA Drive › Physiology Middletown + Harlem (Previous Years) › Physio Exam 2 › Physio Exam 2 › Physiology I Exam 2 TA Review.pptx · 63: A) Phase 4- Funny Na+ channels open B) Phase 0- Influx of Ca2+ C) Phase 3- Efflux of K+
Correct key: Ventricular AP: A) Phase 4 – resting potential held near E_K by K+ efflux (I_K1); B) Phase 0 – fast Na+ influx; C) Phase 1 – Na+ channels inactivate, transient K+ efflux; D) Phase 2 – L-type Ca2+ influx balancing K+ efflux (plateau); E) Phase 3 – Ca2+ channels close, K+ efflux repolarizes. The figure is a ventricular (fast) action potential with five labels A–E, so the first key (phases 4,0,1,2,3) is right. The second key (funny Na+/Ca2+ upstroke/K+) belongs to the TA's SA-node exercise and was mis-merged.
WhyIn a ventricular action potential, rest (4) is held by K⁺ efflux, the upstroke (0) is fast Na⁺ influx, and the notch (1) is Na⁺ inactivation with transient K⁺ efflux. The plateau (2) balances L-type Ca²⁺ influx against K⁺ efflux, and repolarization (3) is K⁺ efflux after Ca²⁺ channels close.
ConceptMatching: ventricular AP phases 4, 0, 1, 2, 3 with their ion movements

SA → Internodal tracts → AV → BOH → BB → PFs Which of these tracts/areas demonstrate automaticity?
AnswerAll of the conducting tracts are capable of demonstrating automaticity.
WhyEvery part of the specialized conduction system has an unstable phase 4 and thus automaticity, but the faster SA node keeps the slower latent pacemakers overdrive-suppressed.
Explanation from the source
Then why does the SA node only drive heart rate (assuming NSR)? It’s the principle of override suppression. Think of it like this, all of these cells have a phase 4 slope though it is less steep (slower) relative to the SA node and an action potential “from above” will propagate there to cause depolarization. That is, it depolarizes due to a propagating potential, and not intrinsic firing. When this happens, after each area’s respective repolarization, the “clock will restart” in terms of the time from then for the slope of phase 4 to reach threshold. Since the slope is greatest (fastest) in SA, it usually is going to win and override automaticity potential in all downstream areas!
ConceptWhich conduction tissues show automaticity

308
SNS effects? Chronotropic? Inotropic? Dromotropic?
AnswerWhat effects does the SNS have? All though B1 receptors!! Positive chronotropic effect mediated by increased If (funny current; increase slope of phase 4 in SA node) and increased Ca++ channel activity and Ca++ sequestering inside cell (allows for larger gradient to develop during repolarization). Positive inotropic effect mediated by changes in calcium handling previously noted. NE/E stimulate GPCR with stimulatory alpha subunit activating adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP, activating PKA and ultimately phosphorylating target proteins. Phosphorylation effects include increased Ca++ conductance during depolarization, increased Ca release during Ca induced Ca release and increased Ca sequestering by SERCA pumps during repolarization. Finally, positive dromotropic effects. This means conduction velocity is increased. Through the aforementioned mechanisms, the gradient is larger which decreases time to full depolarization and repolarization is faster.
WhySympathetic NE acts on β1 (Gs → cAMP → PKA) to raise heart rate (steeper SA phase 4 via ↑I_f and ↑I_Ca), contractility (more Ca²⁺ entry, release and SERCA uptake) and AV conduction velocity.
ConceptSympathetic (β1) effects on heart: + chronotropy, + inotropy, + dromotropy and mechanisms
Slides
309
PSNS effects? Chronotropic? Inotropic? Dromotropic?
AnswerWhat about the PSNS? All through M2 receptors!! Negative chronotropic effect mediated by decreased If (funny current; decreased slope of phase 4 in SA node) and decreased Ca++ channel activity AND K-Ach channel activation which increases K+ efflux during phase 4 leading to hyperpolarization (relative to “normal”). Inotropic effects are MINIMAL!!! This is because there is minimal PSNS innervation of the majority of cardiac tissue. The atria do have some PSNS innervation, but the effect on overall contractility of the heart is really determined by the ventricles. Thus, there could be some negative inotropic effects on the atria, but they are really quite negligible. More important is to think of the SNS and PSNS as the gas and brakes, respectively. In the very strong majority of situations, if we increase outflow of one, we decrease outflow of the other…so, if PSNS outflow is up, it is likely that SNS outflow is down…thus, indirectly, you’ve also removed some SNS influence which has a negative inotropic effect. How are the PSNS effects (in the atria) mediated? It’s simply the opposite of what you see with SNS. Ach activates GPCR with inhibitory alpha subunit…decreased or dephosphorylation of target proteins resulting in decrease Ca++ ion activation and decreased Ca reuptake (SERCA pumps/Ca-ATPase). Finally, what about dromotropic effects? Decreased Ca++ channel activity and increased K-Ach channel activity decrease conduction velocity and increase repolarization time.
WhyVagal ACh acts on M2 (Gi, ↓cAMP) to slow heart rate (↓I_f, ↓I_Ca and K⁺-ACh hyperpolarization of the SA node) and AV conduction, but reduces contractility only in the atria, which have the vagal innervation.
ConceptParasympathetic (M2) effects: − chronotropy, minimal inotropy, − dromotropy and mechanisms

When a coronary artery is occluded the K+ concentration rises in the interstitial fluid of the ischemic region (i.e., the region deprived of its blood supply) of the ventricular myocardium. What effect does the elevated K+ concentration in the interstitial fluid have on the resting membrane potential of myocardial cells in the ischemic zone? What effect does the change in resting membrane potential have on the propagation of the cardiac impulse? Why?
AnswerThe depolarization increases Na+ channel inactivation. Thus, fewer Na+ channels are available for activation. The upstroke of the action potential is less steep than normal, and the amplitude is diminished. However, repolarization is actually faster! The velocity of propagation varies directly with these parameters
WhyRaised extracellular K+ depolarizes the resting membrane potential, which inactivates fast Na+ channels, so the phase 0 upstroke is slower and smaller and conduction velocity in the ischemic zone falls.

A 63-year-old man suddenly felt a crushing pain beneath his sternum. He became weak and began to sweat profusely. He called his physician, who advised him to go to the hospital immediately by ambulance. The tests made at the hospital confirmed his physician’s belief that the patient had suffered a heart attack; that is, a major coronary artery had suddenly become occluded. About one hour after the coronary artery became occluded, conduction in the bundle of His ceased abruptly. The conduction block persisted for several days. At approximately what rates would the atria and ventricles beat after the His bundles had been completely blocked? Where do the impulses originate that initiate the atrial and ventricular contractions in such a patient with complete AV block?
AnswerWhen conduction in the AV node or Bundle of His is blocked, the atrial and ventricular rhythms are dissociated. The atrial rhythm will be set by the SA node, usually 60-90 beats/min. The ventricular rhythm will be set by the Purkinje fibers, in the range of 20-30 beats/min.
WhyIn complete heart block atria and ventricles are dissociated: the SA node still drives the atria at about 60–90/min, while a latent Purkinje pacemaker drives the ventricles at about 20–30/min.
ConceptComplete His block: atrial and ventricular rates and origins

An 80-year-old man had problems with his AV conduction system, and his cardiologist decided that an artificial pacemaker was required. Immediately after the pacemaker had been installed, the cardiologist tested the effects of different pacing frequencies to determine the optimal settings for the patient. Some of the results were as follows: When the heart was paced at 60 beats/min, the patient’s stroke volume was 80 ml, his cardiac output was 4.8 L/min, and his total peripheral resistance was 20 mm Hg/L/min. When the heart was paced at 100 beats/min, the stroke volume was 48 ml, his cardiac output was 4.8 L/min, and his total peripheral resistance was 20 mm Hg/L/min. What directional changes in the arterial systolic, diastolic, and pulse pressure would you expect when the paced heart was switched from 60 to 100 beats/min?
AnswerWith a lower stroke volume, you would expect systolic pressure to be decreased (less volume in aorta w/ each beat). However, diastolic pressure is actually slightly higher (less diastolic time with decreased time between ventricular contractions). Remember, mean arterial pressure was the same. With a lower systolic and higher diastolic pressure, the pulse pressure is lower (SBP-DBP).
WhyMAP = CO × TPR = 4.8 × 20 = 96 mm Hg at both rates, but the smaller SV at 100/min lowers systolic pressure and the shorter diastole lowers diastolic run-off, raising diastolic pressure, so pulse pressure falls.
ConceptPacing 60 → 100/min at same CO: systolic ↓, diastolic ↑, pulse pressure ↓

Months later, Nicholas is brought to the ER on your EM rotation after accidentally ingesting 5 of his grandma’s prescription pills and passing out. He is bradycardic, hypotensive, and has edematous extremities. His grandmother brought her prescription bottle to the office which read “metoprolol”. You know from your pharmacology class that this is a Beta-1 receptor selective blocker. After administering IV fluids and isoproterenol (non-selective beta receptor stimulator), Nicholas recovers. Mechanistically, which of these were a direct effect of the medication that Nicholas took?

  2. B. Increased constriction of both pupils
  3. C. Decrease in cleavage of IP3 in the heart
  4. D. Constriction of bronchioles
  5. E. Decrease in cAMP production in the heart

WhyMetoprolol blocks β1 receptors, which couple to Gs → adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP production in the heart falls, lowering heart rate and contractility.

Part 1: The patient has beta receptor antagonist poisoning. Metoprolol is a Beta-1 selective blocker. Decrease in cAMP production in the heart would occur because Beta-1 receptors use a Gs pathway, which utilizes adenylate cyclase and ATP to produce cAMP. If the drug poisoning was due to a non-selective beta blocker, then answer D would be correct as well. Beta-2 is responsible for airway dilation (think fight or flight, needing to increase airflow).
ConceptMetoprolol (β1 blocker) direct effect: ↓ cAMP production in the heart

  2. B. Prolongs the repolarization phase by blocking potassium channels.

As such, it takes longer to reach the peak of the action potential because it occurs more gradually as represented by the dotted red line in the image on the left. A person’s electrocardiogram (ECG) has no P wave but has a normal QRS complex and a normal T wave. Therefore, his pacemaker is located in the
  1. A. sinoatrial (SA) node
  2. B. atrioventricular (AV) node
  3. C. bundle of His
  4. D. Purkinje system
  5. E. ventricular muscle
AnswerB. atrioventricular (AV) node
WhyA missing P wave means the atria are not activated by the SA node, while a normal QRS and T mean the ventricles still depolarize through the normal His–Purkinje path, so the pacemaker is the AV node (junctional rhythm).
Explanation from the source
The answer is B [III A]. The absent P wave indicates that the atrium is not depolarizing and, therefore, the pacemaker cannot be in the sinoatrial (SA) node. Because the QRS and T waves are normal, depolarization and repolarization of the ventricle must be proceeding in the normal sequence. This situation can occur if the pacemaker is located in the atrioventricular (AV) node. If the pacemaker were located in the bundle of His or in the Purkinje system, the ventricles would activate in an abnormal sequence (depending on the exact location of the pacemaker) and the QRS wave would have an abnormal configuration. Ventricular muscle does not have pacemaker properties.
ConceptNo P wave, normal QRS: pacemaker location

  4. D. an atrial muscle cell

Explanation from the source
The answer is E [Chapter 3, III B; Figures 3.4 and 3.5]. The action potential shown is characteristic of ventricular muscle, with a stableresting membrane potential and a long plateau phase of almost 300 msec. Action potentials in skeletal cells are much shorter (only a few milliseconds). Smooth muscle action potentials would be superimposed on fluctuating baseline potentials (slow waves). Sinoatrial (SA) cells of the heart have spontaneous depolarization (pacemaker activity) rather than a stableresting potential. Atrial muscle cells of the heart have a much shorter plateau phase and a much shorter overall duration.

Questions 38–41 Use the diagram of an action potential to answer the following questions. Phase 0 of the action potential shown is produced by an
  1. A. inward K+ current
  2. B. inward Na+ current
  3. C. inward Ca2+ current
  4. D. outward Na+ current
  5. E. outward Ca2+ current
AnswerB. inward Na+ current
WhyVentricular phase 0 is the rapid upstroke from opening of fast voltage-gated Na+ channels, an inward Na+ current that drives the membrane toward E_Na.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B [Chapter 3, III C 1 a]. Depolarization, as in phase 0, is caused by an inward current (defined as the movement of positive charge into the cell). The inward current during phase 0 of the ventricular muscle action potential is caused by opening of Na+ channels in the ventricular muscle cell membrane, movement of Na+ into the cell, and depolarization of the membrane potential toward the Na+ equilibrium potential (approximately +65 mV). In sinoatrial (SA) cells, phase 0 is caused by an inward Ca2+ current.

Questions 38–41 Use the diagram of an action potential to answer the following questions. Phase 2, the plateau phase, of the action potential shown
  1. A. is the result of Ca2+ flux out of the cell
  2. B. increases in duration as heart rate increases
  3. C. corresponds to the effective refractory period
  4. D. is the result of approximately equal inward and outward currents
  5. E. is the portion of the action potential when another action potential can most easily be elicited
AnswerD. is the result of approximately equal inward and outward currents
WhyThe plateau (phase 2) is a stable potential because inward L-type Ca2+ current and outward K+ current are about equal.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D [Chapter 3, III B 1 c]. Because the plateau phase is a period of stablemembrane potential, by definition, the inward and outward currents are equal and balance each other. Phase 2 is the result of opening of Ca2+ channels and inward, not outward, Ca2+ current. In this phase, the cells are refractory to the initiation of another action potential. Phase 2 corresponds to the absolute refractory period, rather than the effective refractory period (which is longer than the plateau). As heart rate increases, the duration of the ventricular action potential decreases, primarily by decreasing the duration of phase 2.
ConceptPlateau (phase 2) = approximately equal inward (Ca²⁺) and outward (K⁺) currents

7. Mr Green, a 54-year-old banker, had a cardiac transplant 6 months ago. His current blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg and heart rate is 100 bpm. Which of the following drugs would have the least effect on Mr Green's heart rate?
  1. A. Albuterol
  2. B. Epinephrine
  3. C. Isoproterenol
  4. D. Norepinephrine
  5. E. Phenylephrine
AnswerE. Phenylephrine
WhyA transplanted heart is denervated, so phenylephrine, a pure α1 agonist with no direct β1 action, cannot change its rate, because its usual reflex bradycardia needs intact vagal nerves.
Explanation from the source
Heart transplantation involves cutting of the autonomic nerves to the heart. As a result, autonomic nerve endings degenerate, and cardiac transmitter stores are absent for 2 years or longer after surgery. Therefore, indirect-acting sympathomimetics are ineffective in changing heart rate. All the drugs listed are direct-acting, and all but phenylephrine have significant effects on β receptors. Phenylephrine usually causes reflex bradycardia, which requires intact vagal innervation. The answer is E. (Note that denervation may result in upregulation of both β1 and β2 receptors so that direct-acting β agonists may have a greater than normal effect.)
ConceptDenervated transplanted heart: phenylephrine (α1) has least effect on heart rate

During a clinical rotation through the cardiac intensive care unit of the hospital, you are asked to discuss the control of heart rate by the autonomic nervous system. Which of the following best describes the primary function of sympathetic stimulation on the heart?
  1. (A) Constriction of coronary arteries
  2. (B) Decreases heart rate
  3. (C) Increases heart rate
  4. (D) Initiates cardiac muscle contraction
  5. (E) Reduces the force of muscle contraction
Answer(C) Increases heart rate
WhySympathetic NE acts on SA-node β1 receptors (Gs, ↑cAMP) to steepen phase 4 depolarization, so its primary cardiac effect is increased heart rate.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Increases heart rate. The cardiac plexus innervating the heart is composed of (1) sympathetic nerve fibers originating from the lateral horn of spinal cord segments T1 to T6 and (2) parasympathetic nerve fibers from the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X). These autonomic nerve fibers terminate at the sinoatrial (SA) and atrioventricular (AV) nodes of the conducting system of the heart and extend onto the coronary arteries. Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate, force of contraction, and blood flow through dilated coronary arteries (support for increased heart activity). By contrast, parasympathetic stimulation slows heart rate, reduces the force of muscle contraction, and reduces blood flow to the heart (vasoconstriction). None of the other choices describe the primary function of sympathetic stimulation on the heart. Keywords: Autonomic nervous system, sympathetic division, cardiac nervous plexus
ConceptEffect of sympathetic stimulation on the heart

SA → Internodal tracts → AV → BOH → BB → PFs • Which of these tracts/areas demonstrate automaticity?
AnswerAll of the conducting tracts are capable of demonstrating automaticity.
Explanation from the source
Then why does the SA node only drive heart rate (assuming NSR)? It’s the principle of override suppression. Think of it like this, all of these cells have a phase 4 slope though it is less steep (slower) relative to the SA node and an action potential “from above” will propagate there to cause depolarization. That is, it depolarizes due to a propagating potential, and not intrinsic firing. When this happens, after each area’s respective repolarization, the “clock will restart” in terms of the time from then for the slope of phase 4 to reach threshold. Since the slope is greatest (fastest) in SA, it usually is going to win and override automaticity potential in all downstream areas!
ConceptWhich conduction tissues show automaticity

  4. D) Sympathetic stimulation decreases the refractory period of the SA node, allowing for more frequent firing, while parasympathetic stimulation increases the threshold for depolarization, making it more difficult for the SA node to initiate action potentials.
AnswerB. The release of norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve endings enhances automaticity of the SA node by increasing cAMP levels, resulting in increased heart rate, whereas acetylcholine release from parasympathetic fibers decreases cAMP levels, slowing conduction through the AV node.
WhyNorepinephrine (β1, Gs) raises cAMP in the SA node, increasing I_f and Ca²⁺ current to steepen phase 4 and speed HR, while ACh (M2, Gi) lowers cAMP and slows AV-node conduction.
ConceptNE ↑ cAMP → ↑ SA automaticity; ACh ↓ cAMP → slower AV conduction

While conducting research on the electrical properties of the heart, scientists measure action potential conduction velocity at four different points within normal cardiac muscle. The following results are obtained, expressed in terms of speed of conduction. Point 1 - 1.1 m/s Point 2 - 0.05 m/s Point 3 - 2.2 m/s Point 4- 0.3 m/s Which of these points plays the largest role in allowing time for the ventricles to fill with blood, and what is the name of the site?
Show figure
  1. a) Point 2, SA Node
  2. b) Point 3, Bundle of His
  3. c) Point 2, AV Node
  4. d) Point 2, SA Node
  5. e) Point 1, Ventricle
  6. f) Point 1, Atria
Answerc) Point 2, AV Node
WhyThe AV node conducts slowest of all cardiac tissue (about 0.01–0.05 m/s), producing the AV delay that gives the ventricles time to fill before they depolarize.
Explanation from the source
Conduction through the AV node (called AV delay) requires almost one-half of the total conduction time through the myocardium. The reason for the AV delay is that, of all the myocardial tissues, conduction velocity in the AV node is slowest (0.01–0.05 m/s), making conduction time the longest (100 ms). None of these numbers are important. You should know the order from fastest to slowest though, and the reasoning why the AV nodal conduction velocity is so slow (it allows the ventricles time to fill!)
ConceptSlowest conduction (0.05 m/s) = AV node: gives time for ventricular filling

Gentle neck massage just below the angle of the right mandible produces immediate improvement of her condition. Her heart rate is now 75 beats per minute and her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. This maneuver improved the patient's symptoms by…
  1. A. Decreasing the baroreceptor firing rate
  2. B. Increasing sympathetic output to the SA node
  3. C. Prolonging the AV node refractory period
  4. D. Prolonging ventricular myocardium refractory period
  5. E. Decreasing atrial contractility

WhyCarotid sinus massage stretches the baroreceptors and raises vagal (M2) tone, which slows AV nodal conduction and prolongs the AV node refractory period, interrupting the re-entrant tachycardia.
Explanation from the source
This is describing a carotid sinus massage, which increases baroreceptor firing and increases the parasympathetic influence on the heart. Remember decreased firing causes an increase in sympathetic tone, and vice-versa. When you give a carotid massage you are applying tension to the carotid sinus walls, mimicking high blood pressure. While atrial contractility would indeed decrease as a result of increased parasympathetic tone, this is unlikely to affect her symptoms. Decreasing AV nodal conduction velocity through parasympathetic tone and allowing the ventricles more time to fill will help reduce her symptoms the most.
ConceptCarotid sinus massage ends SVT by prolonging the AV node refractory period

4. A person’s electrocardiogram (ECG) has no P wave, but has a normal QRS complex and a normal T wave. Therefore, his pacemaker is located in the
  1. (A) sinoatrial (SA) node
  2. (B) atrioventricular (AV) node
  3. (C) bundle of His
  4. (D) Purkinje system
  5. (E) ventricular muscle
AnswerB. atrioventricular (AV) node
Explanation from the source
The absent P wave indicates that the atrium is not depolarizing and, therefore, the pacemaker cannot be in the sinoatrial (SA) node. Because the QRS and T waves are normal, depolarization and repolarization of the ventricle must be proceed- ing in the normal sequence. This situation can occur if the pacemaker is located in the atrioventricular (AV) node. If the pacemaker were located in the bundle of His or in the Purkinje system, the ventricles would activate in an abnormal sequence (depending on the exact location of the pacemaker) and the QRS wave would have an abnormal configu- ration. Ventricular muscle does not have pacemaker properties.
ConceptNo P wave, normal QRS: pacemaker location

The PR interval includes the P wave (atrial depolarization) and the PR segment, which represents con- duction through the atrioventricular (AV) node; during this phase, the ventricles are not yet depolarized. The ST segment is the only isoelectric period when the entire ventricle is depolarized.

Which of the following is consistent with the ECG tracing shown below?

  2. B. First-degree heart block
  3. C. Second-degree heart block
  4. D. Third-degree heart block
  5. E. Tachycardia

WhyFirst-degree heart block is a PR interval longer than 0.20 s with every P wave still followed by a QRS, reflecting slowed conduction through the AV node.
Explanation from the source
The answer is b. (Guyton, pp 134-136.) The only abnormality in the Tac hycard ia ECG illustrated is a prolonged PR interval representing a delay in the Propagation of the cardiac action potential from the atria to the ventricles. This is defined as a first-degree heart block. The normal PR interval is between 0.12 and 0.20 s. In a second-degree heart block, some of the P waves are not propagated into the ventricles, but every QRS complex is preceded by a P wave. In third-degree heart block, the atria and ventricles are electrically isolated and thus beat independently. The ventricular rate during a third-degree heart block is typically about 40 beats per minute. Tachycardia is a rapid heart rate above 100 beats per minute, and bradycardia is a slow heart rate below 60 beats per minute. The heart rate from which this ECG tracing was obtained was 75 beats per minute.
ConceptEKG strip with long PR, every P followed by QRS → first-degree heart block

Increasing vagal stimulation of the heart will cause an increase in
  1. A. Heart rate
  2. B. PR interval
  3. C. Ventricular contractility
  4. D. Ejection fraction
  5. E. Cardiac output
AnswerB. PR interval
WhyVagal ACh acting on M2 receptors slows AV nodal conduction (negative dromotropy), lengthening the PR interval.
Explanation from the source
The answer is b. (Guyton, pp 134-136.) The vagal fibers innervating Cardiac output the heart stimulate intracardiac postganglionic fibers, which release acetylcholine (ACh). The postganglionic fibers innervate the SA and AV nodal fibers. ACh causes a decrease in the rate of phase-4 depolarization, thus slowing the heart, and a decrease in conduction velocity through the AV node, thus increasing the PR interval. ACh also causes a slight decrease in contractility. Decreasing the heart rate increases the amount of time available for ventricular filling and thus increases end-diastolic volume. However, the end-systolic volume will be somewhat elevated because of the slight decrease in contractility and increase in afterload. Thus, the ejection fraction will remain the same or decrease slightly.

Propranolol has which of the following effects?
  1. A. Decreases heart rate
  2. B. Increases left ventricular ejection fraction
  3. C. Increases stroke volume
  4. D. Decreases splanchnic vascular resistance
  5. E. Decreases cutaneous vascular resistance
AnswerA. Decreases heart rate
WhyPropranolol blocks β1 receptors on the SA node, removing sympathetic acceleration of phase 4 depolarization, so heart rate falls.
Explanation from the source
Propranolol, a β-adrenergic antagonist, blocks all sympathetic effects that are mediated by a β1 or β2 receptor. The sympathetic effect on the sinoatrial (SA) node is to increase heart rate via a β1 receptor; therefore, propranolol decreases heart rate. Ejection fraction reflects ventricular contractility, which is another effect of β1 receptors; thus, propranolol decreases contractility, ejection fraction, and stroke volume. Splanchnic and cutaneous resistance are mediated by α1 receptors.
ConceptPropranolol effect: ↓ heart rate

531
Which of these tracts/areas demonstrate automaticity?
AnswerAll of the conducting tracts are capable of demonstrating automaticity.
Explanation from the source
All of the conducting tracts are capable of demonstrating automaticity. Then why does the SA node only drive heart rate (assuming NSR)? It’s the principle of override suppression. Think of it like this, all of these cells have a phase 4 slope though it is less steep (slower) relative to the SA node and an action potential “from above” will propagate there to cause depolarization. That is, it depolarizes due to a propagating potential, and not intrinsic firing. When this happens, after each area’s respective repolarization, the “clock will restart” in terms of the time from then for the slope of phase 4 to reach threshold. Since the slope is greatest (fastest) in SA, it usually is going to win and override automaticity potential in all downstream areas!
ConceptWhich conduction tissues show automaticity

His father is deceased from unknown cause of sudden cardiac death at age 38. The patient is up to date with vaccinations. Vitals are stable and he is saturating 99% on room air. Mild end-expiratory wheezing is auscultated. Laboratory workup is unrevealing. The patient is given a single dose of azithromycin and ondansetron. He is monitored in the emergency room. The patient’s respiratory symptoms improve, and he is prescribed a short-acting inhaled beta-agonist on discharge. Four hours later, the patient returns to the emergency room with his mother for acute worsening of shortness of breath. Electrocardiogram findings from lead II are shown below. Which of the following most likely explains the cause of this patient’s return to the emergency department?
  1. A. Decreased inward calcium current in pacemaker cells
  2. B. Decreased inward calcium current in cardiomyocytes
  3. C. Decreased inward sodium current in cardiomyocytes
  4. D. Decreased outward potassium current in cardiomyocytes
  5. E. Increased outward potassium current in pacemaker cells
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyD. Decreased outward potassium current in cardiomyocytes
WhyAzithromycin and ondansetron block the hERG (I_Kr) delayed-rectifier channel, decreasing outward K⁺ current in phase 3, prolonging the QT interval and risking torsades in congenital long QT.
ConceptDrug-induced long QT: ↓ outward K⁺ current in cardiomyocytes

P elevation represents the wave that spreads from the SA node to atria, causing depolarization. The R wave represents the ventricular depolarization. S depression represents spread of the ventricular depolarization to purkinje fibers in the walls of the ventricles. T wave are ventricular repolarization.
ConceptEKG wave of SA-node/atrial depolarization

614Borderline
A patient presents with primary aldosteronism caused by an aldosterone secreting tumor resulting in severe hypokalemia (low potassium concentration in the blood). Why is the patient at a greater risk for arrhythmias?
  1. A. Low intracellular potassium results in increased likelihood of generating action potentials
  2. B. Low extracellular potassium results in a shift of the Nernst Equilibrium Potential of K+ to an even more negative value
  3. C. Low intracellular potassium results in a shift of the Nernst Equilibrium Potential of K+ to less negative value
  4. D. Low extracellular potassium results in a shift of the Nernst Equilibrium Potential of K+ to a less negative value
  5. E. Just eat a banana and you’ll be fine!
AnswerB. Low extracellular potassium results in a shift of the Nernst Equilibrium Potential of K+ to an even more negative value
WhyLow extracellular K⁺ widens the K⁺ gradient, so the Nernst potential for K⁺ (E_K) becomes more negative; hypokalemia also slows repolarization (long QT, U waves), favoring arrhythmias.
Explanation from the source
Hypokalemia = low extracellular K+ concentration Since there’s a high concentration of K+ intracellularly and there is now an even LOWER concentration of K+ extracellularly, the driving force for diffusion of K+ has increased, resulting in a hyperpolarized state K+ “wants” to leave the cell even MORE now which will cause the cell to become more negative relative to before since positive charges are leaving the cell Hyperpolarized cells are unable to reach threshold as frequently as they should, thus resulting in a lack of consistent action potentials and a greater risk for cardiac arrhythmias
Old Physiology Exam 1 (Nernst/RMP) review item framed as cardiac arrhythmia risk in hypokalemia; plasma K+ effects on the cardiac action potential are IN (L20/21 Problem Set 7), the Nernst reasoning itself is Foundations.

A 25-year-old female presents to the emergency room with dyspnea and palpitations. She states that she believes she may be having a panic-attack. She reports that she was walking her dog when suddenly she began to feel lightheaded and short of breath. She denies any family history of heart disease. Telemetry monitoring reveals an irregularly irregular heart rate of 134/min. Blood pressure is 138/54, respiratory rate is 14/min, blood glucose is 84 mg/dL. Fine tremors are observed in the distal phalanges. Electrocardiogram is performed and shown. Initial labs reveal a significantly decreased thyroid-stimulating hormone level. Which of the following locations is likely a source of aberrant electrical foci contributing to this patient’s symptoms?
  1. ⚪ A. Cavotricuspid isthmus of right atrium
  2. ⚪ B. Superior subendocardial right atrium
  3. ⚪ C. Membranous portion of interventricular septum
  4. ⚪ D. Left posterior atrioventricular groove
  5. ⚪ E. Pulmonary vein ostia of left atrium
  6. ⚪ F. Pulmonary artery root of right ventricle
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyE. Pulmonary vein ostia of left atrium
WhyAtrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves), which hyperthyroidism promotes, is usually triggered by ectopic foci in atrial muscle sleeves at the pulmonary vein ostia of the left atrium.
Irregularly irregular tachycardia is atrial fibrillation, which L20/21 teaches (fibrillatory baseline, no PR, shortened atrial refractory period). The lecture does not teach that the triggers sit at the pulmonary-vein ostia; that is ablation-level detail.

A 17-year-old male presents to the emergency room for 8/10 chest pain that began during a soccer practice a few hours earlier. He states that he has experienced chest discomfort and shortness of breath in the past with sports activity and had previously been diagnosed with asthma 3 years earlier. He states that he finds little improvement in his symptoms when using his albuterol inhaler. He denies any other past medical or surgical history. He states that his father and first cousin are both deceased from “heart problems” in their early thirties. He states that he vapes occasionally and denies any other substance use. Blood pressure is 108/58 mmHg, heart rate is 76/min and regular, oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. The point of maximal impulse appears to be modestly shifted laterally beyond the midclavicular line. A 2/6 crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is auscultated at the lower left sternal border. The murmur is accentuated with standing. Pulmonary auscultation reveals clear lung sounds bilaterally with no wheezing observed. ECG reveals a regular rhythm with left axis deviation and deep Q waves in leads I, II, III, aVF and V5-V6 are observed. A transthoracic echocardiogram and cardiac MRI are performed. The patient is subsequently prescribed a medication and restricted from further sports activity on discharge. Which of the following mechanisms of action would most likely be consistent with the medication given?
  1. A. Activation of β1-receptors in myocardial cells
  2. B. Activation of guanylyl cyclase at venous and coronary vessels
  3. C. Inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase in myocardial cells
  4. D. Inhibition of phosphodiesterase-5 enzymes in vascular smooth muscle
  5. E. Inhibition of Na+/K+/Cl- co-transporters in the loop of Henle
  6. F. Non-selective inhibition of β-receptors systemically
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyF. Non-selective inhibition of β-receptors systemically
WhyA non-selective β-blocker in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy slows HR and lowers contractility, lengthening diastolic filling and enlarging the LV cavity, which lessens outflow obstruction and O₂ demand.
A nonselective beta blocker is on the drug list and slows the SA node. Hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy maneuvers (murmur louder on standing) are not on the physiology slides.

Maria Rodriguez, a 48-year-old Latina woman, presented to the clinic reporting a several-month history of episodic "spells" of racing and pounding of her heart, along with symptoms such as sweating, throbbing headache, cold hands and feet, visual disturbances, nausea, and vomiting. During the examination, her blood pressure was significantly elevated at 220/120 mmHg, and her heart rate increased to 110/min. The results of a 24-hour urinary VMA test, a metabolite of epinephrine and norepinephrine, returned positive. A subsequent CT scan confirmed the presence of a 3-cm mass on her right adrenal gland, leading to the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. After appropriate pharmacological interventions, surgery was performed. Maria recovered fully; her blood pressure returned to normal, and her other symptoms disappeared. Integrated Understanding: How do the reported symptoms align with the physiological effects of increased levels of epinephrine and norepinephrine in the body?
AnswerEach symptom is a catecholamine receptor effect: beta1 (heart) -> tachycardia (racing, +chronotropy) and pounding (+inotropy); alpha1 vasoconstriction -> cold extremities, raised TPR and severe hypertension (BP = CO x TPR), cerebral vasoconstriction/hypertension -> throbbing headache; sweating via sympathetic (muscarinic/alpha) sweat-gland stimulation and increased metabolic rate; alpha1 radial iris contraction (mydriasis), beta2 ciliary relaxation (loss of accommodation) and ocular vasoconstriction -> visual disturbances; beta2/alpha2 GI wall relaxation + alpha1 sphincter contraction (plus central CTZ effect) -> nausea/vomiting.
WhyPheochromocytoma symptoms are catecholamine receptor effects: β1 gives racing, pounding beats; α1 vasoconstriction gives cold extremities, severe hypertension and headache; sympathetic actions on sweat glands, eye and gut give the rest.
Racing heart and cold extremities are β1 and α1; sweating and the rest of the symptom list are gland and metabolic effects (MSK II).

AnswerRacing/pounding heart: excessive beta1 stimulation (+chronotropy, +inotropy). Sweating: excessive muscarinic and alpha-adrenergic stimulation of sweat glands plus increased metabolic rate. Throbbing headache: alpha1-mediated cerebral vasoconstriction (reduced flow) and the elevated blood pressure.
WhyIn pheochromocytoma, excess β1 stimulation gives racing, pounding beats, sympathetic stimulation of sweat glands gives sweating, and α1 cerebral vasoconstriction with severe hypertension gives the throbbing headache.
Racing heart and cold extremities are β1 and α1; sweating and the rest of the symptom list are gland and metabolic effects (MSK II).

The results of a 24-hour test for urinary VMA (a metabolite of epinephrine and norepinephrine) were positive and a CT scan confirmed that he had a 3-cm mass on his right adrenal gland. A diagnosis of pheochromocytoma was made. Q3. Discuss the possible pathophysiological bases of this patient's symptoms. What autonomic receptors are involved in each of his symptoms?
AnswerAll symptoms are actions of catecholamines. Heart (beta1): increased HR, contractility and conduction velocity
WhyIn pheochromocytoma, β1 on the heart raises rate and contractility (palpitations), α1 constricts skin and cerebral vessels and raises TPR (cold hands, headache, hypertension), and gut-wall relaxation with sphincter contraction causes nausea and vomiting.

-> racing (palpitations) and pounding. Blood vessels (alpha1): vasoconstriction in most beds -> decreased cutaneous flow (pale, cold hands/feet) and decreased cerebral flow (headache), plus increased TPR -> hypertension. GI tract: relaxation of smooth muscle walls (beta2, alpha2) and contraction of sphincters (alpha1) slow chyme -> nausea and vomiting. (Also: sweating via sympathetic cholinergic/alpha stimulation of sweat glands; visual disturbance via alpha1 radial-muscle mydriasis.) Map each sign to receptor: beta1 heart, alpha1 vessels/sphincters/radial iris, beta2/alpha2 GI wall relaxation.
Heart and vessels are β1 and α1; sweating and the other symptoms are gland and metabolic effects (MSK II).

One of her friends acts fast an injected her with epinephrine. What effects does this have on her heart rate (SA Node) and bronchioles?

Clinical Case 1: A 42-year-old male presented to his doctor complaining of a several-month history of racing and pounding of his heart, sweating, throbbing headache, cold hands and feet, visual disturbances, nausea and vomiting. On examination, his blood pressure was severely elevated at 200/110 and heart rate was increased at 110/min. Asked for the sweat-gland receptor, answer muscarinic.
WhyIn pheochromocytoma β1 drives palpitations, α1 vasoconstriction gives cold extremities, headache and hypertension, gut slowing gives nausea, and sweating is mainly sympathetic cholinergic (muscarinic).
Heart and vessels are β1 and α1; sweating and the other symptoms are gland and metabolic effects (MSK II).

AnswerM2 (SA and AV node); M3 (smooth muscle of eye, bronchioles, GI tract, bladder).

Two drugs are infused in separate subjects. Drug X (a direct muscarinic agonist) lowers blood pressure by vasodilation; Drug Y (an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) causes bradycardia, bronchospasm and diarrhea but no vasodilation. What explains the difference in vascular response?
  1. A. Vessels have endothelial M3 receptors but no cholinergic innervation, so only a directly binding agonist can activate them
  2. B. Vascular smooth muscle lacks muscarinic receptors entirely
  3. C. Drug Y does not cross the blood-brain barrier
  4. D. Drug Y is selective for nicotinic receptors
  5. E. Vasodilation requires M2 receptors, which Drug Y cannot reach
AnswerA. Vessels have endothelial M3 receptors but no cholinergic innervation, so only a directly binding agonist can activate them
WhyBlood vessels carry endothelial M3 receptors but no cholinergic innervation, so only a directly acting agonist triggers NO-mediated vasodilation; an AChE inhibitor has no released ACh there to preserve.

Fill out this chart (Receptor | Signaling | Location | Major effects on the body) for M1, M2, M3, A1, A2, B1, B2.
AnswerM1: Gq; CNS, nerves/ganglia, gastric parietal cells & salivary glands (increased secretion/acid). M2: Gi; atria,
WhyM1, M3 and α1 are Gq, M2 and α2 are Gi, and β1 and β2 are Gs; in the circulation M2 slows the heart, M3 dilates via endothelial NO, α1 constricts vessels, α2 cuts NE release, β1 speeds and strengthens the heart and releases renin, and β2 dilates muscle vessels and bronchi.
Explanation from the source
SA and AV node (decreased HR and AV conduction). M3: Gq; glands, smooth muscle (bronchi, GI, bladder detrusor, iris sphincter/ciliary muscle), endothelium (vasodilation via NO release). A1: Gq; vasculature, bladder sphincter/prostate, iris radial muscle (vasoconstriction, increased TPR/BP, mydriasis, urethral sphincter & prostate contraction). A2: Gi; presynaptic nerve terminals, CNS, pancreas, fat, ciliary body (inhibition of NE release, decreased insulin, decreased lipolysis, decreased aqueous humor). B1: Gs; heart (SA/AV node, myocytes) and JG cells (increased HR, contractility, conduction, CO; increased renin). B2: Gs; bronchial, vascular (skeletal muscle/coronary), uterine smooth muscle, liver, pancreas, ciliary body (bronchodilation, vasodilation, decreased diastolic BP, glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis, increased insulin, increased aqueous humor). Mnemonic: M1-M2-M3 = Q-I-Q; alpha1-alpha2-beta1-beta2 = Q-I-S-S. The source answer slide left M1/M2 effects blank; they were filled in (M1 secretion/acid, M2 cardiac slowing).
The chart’s cardiac rows (M2 heart, α1 TPR, β1 heart/renin, endothelial NO) are CP1; eye, bladder, glands, and gut rows are MSK II.

A diagnosis of pheochromocytoma was made. [/] Discuss the possible pathophysiological bases of this patient’s symptoms. What autonomic receptors are involved in each of his symptoms?
AnswerAll of the symptoms can be explained in terms of actions of catecholamines on the various organ systems.[/] In the [/]heart[/], catecholamines have three major effects mediated by [/]β[/]1 receptors: increased heart rate, increased contractility or force of contraction, and increased conduction velocity. Excess catecholamines caused the sensation that the heart was racing (palpitations) and pounding (increased contractility).[/] In [/]blood vessels[/], catecholamines through [/]α[/]1 receptors cause vasoconstriction in most vascular beds. This causes decreased cutaneous blood flow, leading to pale and cold skin, and decreased cerebral blood flow, leading to headaches.[/] In the [/]GI tract[/], relaxation of smooth muscle walls ([/]β[/]2 and [/]α[/]2 receptors) and contraction of sphincters ([/]α[/]1 receptors) slow the motility of chyme through the system, which can lead to nausea and vomiting. [/]
WhyCatecholamines act on β1 receptors in the heart (palpitations, forceful beats), α1 receptors in arterioles (cold, pale skin, hypertension, headache), and β2/α2 GI wall plus α1 sphincter receptors (slowed motility, nausea, vomiting).
Heart (β1: rate, contractility, conduction) and most vascular beds (α1 constriction) are CP1. GI motility, sweating and the pupil in the same symptom list are MSK II.

A 65-year-old man being treated with a beta-blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor for his heart failure presents to his cardiologist’s office complaining of fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, and a irregular heartbeat. An electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals atrial fibrillation, so his cardiologist adds digoxin to his treatment regimen, but tells the patient that he will need to get his blood drawn to check for low K+ on a regular basis. Hypokalemia will increase the risk and severity of digitalis toxicity because of which of the following?
  1. a. Hypopolarization of cardiac muscle membranes
  2. b. Increased amplitude of cardiac muscle action potentials
  3. c. Increased excitability of cardiac muscle cells
  4. d. Increased inhibition of the Na+ − K+ pump
  5. e. Increased removal of cardiac cytosolic Ca2+ via the Na+ − Ca2+ exchanger
AnswerD. d. Increased inhibition of the Na+ − K+ pump
WhyDigoxin and K⁺ compete for the same binding site on the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so low plasma K⁺ lets more digoxin bind, deepening pump inhibition and toxicity.

Following a cardiac action potential (AP) that results in depolarization, inward Ca2+ current from extracellular fluid (ECF) to intracellular fluid (ICF) occurs via ____________ receptors. Entry of Ca2+ into the cell then triggers the release of more Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum storage occurs via ____________ receptors. This process is known as ____________.
Answerdihydropyridine; ryanodine; Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release
WhyPlateau Ca²⁺ enters through dihydropyridine (L-type) receptors, and this trigger Ca²⁺ opens ryanodine receptors on the SR to release far more — Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release.
Explanation from the source
Following a cardiac action potential (AP) that results in depolarization, inward Ca2+ current from extracellular fluid (ECF) to intracellular fluid (ICF) occurs via dihydropyridine receptors. Entry of Ca2+ into the cell then triggers the release of more Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum storage occurs via ryanodine receptors. This process is known as Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release. NOTE: the magnitude of the tension developed by myocardial cells is proportional to how much Ca2+ is in the cells!! More Ca2+ = longer interaction between actin-myosin
ConceptEC coupling: Ca2+ entry via dihydropyridine (L-type) → SR release via ryanodine = CICR

Which of the following statements describes the effect of the sympathetic nervous system on contractility?

  2. B. Activation of muscarinic receptors increases inward Ca2+ current during the plateau of the AP
  3. C. Its effects ultimately cause a briefer contraction
  4. D. Its receptor is coupled via Gi protein, which leads to an increase in contractility.

WhySympathetic β1 → PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, speeding SERCA reuptake of Ca²⁺ into the SR, so relaxation is faster and each contraction is briefer.
Explanation from the source
A. Dephosphorylation of phospholamban stimulates the Ca+2 ATPase and results in greater uptake and storage of Ca2+ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum → It’s the phosphorylation of phospholamban that stimulates the Ca2+ ATPase B. Activation of muscarinic receptors increases inward Ca2+ current during the plateau of the AP → activation of muscarinic receptors decreases inward Ca2+ current during the plateau of the AP C. Its effects ultimately cause a briefer contraction → CORRECT! This is due to the increased Ca2+ uptake by the SR → causes faster relaxation, which allows more time for refilling, and increases the amount of stored Ca2+ for release on the next heartbeat D. Its receptor is coupled via Gi protein, which leads to an increase in contractility. → via Gs protein
ConceptSympathetic effect on contractility: faster SR Ca2+ reuptake → briefer contraction

  3. C. Has no effect
  4. D. Increases the tension that develops on the next beat
AnswerD. Increases the tension that develops on the next beat

The first beat after an increase in heart rate does NOT show an increase in tension.
  1. A. True
  2. B. False
AnswerA. True
WhyIn the positive staircase (Bowditch) effect, extra Ca²⁺ builds up in the SR over several beats, so the first beat after a rate increase shows no rise in tension.
Explanation from the source
True → CORRECT! Extra Ca2+ has not yet accumulated - on subsequent beats the effect of extra accumulation of Ca2+ by the SR shows an increase in tension When more action potentials occur per unit time, more Ca2+ enters the myocardial cells during the action potential plateaus, more Ca2+ is stored in the SR, more Ca2+ is released from the SR, and greater tension is produced during contraction. Positive Staircase Effect: Increased heart rate increases the force of contraction in a stepwise fashion as the intracellular Ca2+ increases cumulatively over several beats.
ConceptPositive staircase: first beat after ↑HR shows no ↑ tension (True)
