Which of the following is an effect of sympathetic stimulation?
Show figure
  1. a. Alpha-1-mediated increase in heart contractility
  2. b. Beta-1 decreases cAMP and increases heart contractility
  3. c. Beta-2-mediated increase in heart contractility
  4. d. Phosphorylation of phospholamban and increased calcium pumped into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
  5. e. Phosphorylation of phospholamban and decreased calcium pumped into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
AnswerD. d. Phosphorylation of phospholamban and increased calcium pumped into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Explanation from the source
All heart effects for SNS stimulation are going to be mediated through B1 receptors. The effect there is to increase cAMP production. Increased cAMP activates PKA which can phosphorylate target proteins including phospholamban. Phosphorylation of this target causes an INCREASE in the rate of calcium reuptake into the SR. This allows for quicker repolarization as well as creating a greater concentration gradient for subsequent depolarization. In the picture you can see PP-1…this is a phosphatase. You’ve probably learned in biochemistry that active PKA will phosphorylate many protein targets and this includes phosphatases (which dephosphorylate proteins when not phosphorylated themselves). Active PKA phosphorylates phospholamban (PLB; increases SERCA activity) and PP-1 (prevents dephosphorylation of PLB by PP-1)
ConceptSympathetic: phospholamban phosphorylation → ↑ Ca2+ pumped into SR

654
How do cardiac glycosides work?
AnswerCardiac glycosides (e.g. digoxin). How do they work? Through competitive inhibition of the binding site for K on the Na-K pump. Inhibiting the Na-K pump causes the sodium gradient to decrease (less in ECF)….this gradient is the driving force for a Ca-Na exchanger which (through secondary active transport) moves Ca out of the cell. So, with less Ca being moved OUT due to this gradient, intracellular Ca levels rise. AND, intracellular calcium concentrations are the biggest factor determining contractility in myocytes!!

Inhibiting the Na-K pump causes the sodium gradient to decrease (less in ECF)….this gradient is the driving force for a Ca-Na exchanger which (through secondary active transport) moves Ca out of the cell. So, with less Ca being moved OUT due to this gradient, intracellular Ca levels rise. AND, intracellular calcium concentrations are the biggest factor determining contractility in myocytes!!

What is Frank-Starling mechanism and why is it so vital?
Show figure
AnswerIf cardiac muscle sarcomeres are stretched, within limits, they contract more forcibly
Sources disagree on the key:
  • Canvas 2026 › Medical Physiology I › 2025 Fall Cardiology 2 - Discussion Session w Answers.pptx · 37: If cardiac muscle sarcomeres are stretched, within limits, they contract more forcibly
  • Canvas 2026 › Medical Physiology I › 2024 Fall Cardio Physio Exam 2 Review Session w Answers.pptx · 40: Preload will be referred to as several things, EDV and “stretch” of the myocardium. In normal, healthy physiology an increased EDV will mean increased stretch of the ventricular myocytes which creates a more favorable actin/myosin overlap prior to the initiation of contraction. What is the result? More force is generated. This is the Frank Starling mechanism of the heart in a nutshell. It helps to match output from the ventricle with input (venous return). Very important to prevent “backup” of fluid in the CV tree. Preload and the Frank Starling Mechanism of the heart is NOT CONTRACTILITY. When you hear contractility, it has to do with dynamics INDEPENDENT of preload or myocyte stretch. Think back to the effect of Ca++ on contraction…B1 stimulation via NE and the corresponding effects on inotropy are a great example. More on this in a second.
  • Canvas 2026 › Medical Physiology I › 2023 Fall Physio Exam 2 Review Session Part I & II w Answers-1.pptx · 85: If cardiac muscle sarcomeres are stretched, within limits, they contract more forcibly Cardiac Output = Venous Return
  • Canvas 2026 › Medical Physiology I › 2022 Fall Physio Exam 2 Review Session Part I & II w Answers-1.pptx · 84: If cardiac muscle sarcomeres are stretched, within limits, they contract more forcibly Cardiac Output = Venous Return
  • Canvas 2026 › Medical Physiology I › 2021 Fall Physio Exam 2 Review Session Part I w Answers-2.pptx · 48: If cardiac muscle sarcomeres are stretched, within limits, they contract more forcibly Cardiac Output = Venous Return
  • SGA Drive › Mod Exams (Fall 2025) › Cardio-Pulm Exam 2 › Physio-Pharm › Montana › IA › 2025 Fall Physiology I Week 11b (Cardio 2) Lecture Session (w answers).pptx · 31: If cardiac muscle sarcomeres are stretched, within limits, they contract more forcibly
Correct key: Within limits, greater stretch (↑EDV/preload) → more optimal sarcomere length/actin–myosin overlap → more forceful contraction (↑SV), so ventricular output matches venous return (CO = VR) and prevents backup; it is preload-dependent, not a change in contractility.. All three review keys say the same thing at different lengths (L22).
WhyGreater stretch (↑EDV, preload) moves sarcomeres toward optimal actin–myosin overlap so the ventricle contracts more forcefully; this Frank–Starling mechanism makes cardiac output match venous return and prevents back-up.
Explanation from the source
Preload will be referred to as several things, EDV and “stretch” of the myocardium. In normal, healthy physiology an increased EDV will mean increased stretch of the ventricular myocytes which creates a more favorable actin/myosin overlap prior to the initiation of contraction. What is the result? More force is generated. This is the Frank Starling mechanism of the heart in a nutshell. It helps to match output from the ventricle with input (venous return). Very important to prevent “backup” of fluid in the CV tree. Preload and the Frank Starling Mechanism of the heart is NOT CONTRACTILITY. When you hear contractility, it has to do with dynamics INDEPENDENT of preload or myocyte stretch. Think back to the effect of Ca++ on contraction…B1 stimulation via NE and the corresponding effects on inotropy are a great example. More on this in a second. Now, back to Frank Starling really quick. We know that if we increase EDV there will be a corresponding increase in SV. OK. Now, to illustrate contractility, think of a situation where you have an EDV of 100 and SV is 60. Add SNS innervation and now you have a SV of 70 with an EDV of 100 (I know this isn’t a perfect example as there’s other effects of SNS, but just think isolated right now). What happened? With an increase in contractility you get an increase in SV WITHOUT an increase in EDV. It’s independent of EDV. You’ll see this illustrated on the next slide as well.
ConceptFrank–Starling mechanism: ↑ stretch (preload) → ↑ force; matches CO to venous return

A 67-year-old woman with a history of heart failure started on digoxin, a cardiac glycoside, after continuing to have symptoms. Three weeks later, she reports she can walk longer distances without becoming fatigued and her exercise tolerance has improved. During rounds, the attending physician asks you, as a medical student, to explain the cellular mechanism responsible for her improvement. Which of the following best explains the mechanism that is responsible for the increased myocardial contractility?
  1. A. Activation of the Na+/K+ -ATPase increases intracellular K+, stimulating calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  2. B. Inhibition of Na+/K+ -ATPase decreases intracellular K+, directly increasing Ca2+ entry through voltage gated Ca channels.
  3. C. Inhibition of Na+/K+ -ATPase increases intracellular Na+, reducing Na+/Ca2+ exchanger activity and increasing intracellular Ca2+.

AnswerC. Inhibition of Na+/K+ -ATPase increases intracellular Na+, reducing Na+/Ca2+ exchanger activity and increasing intracellular Ca2+.
WhyDigoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, raising intracellular Na⁺, which slows Ca²⁺ extrusion by the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger, so more Ca²⁺ is stored and released and contractility rises.
Explanation from the source
Explanation: Cardiac Glycosides are given to patients with heart failure. Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+ -ATPase, leading to an increase in intracellular Na+. This will impact the function of the Secondary Active Transports by disrupting the electrochemical gradient. The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger in the muscle cell depends on the Na+ gradient to remove Ca2+ from the cell, therefore the reduced Na+ gradient will decrease the chance of Ca2+ from leaving the cell. As a result, Ca2+ is trapped inside the cell and contraction will be sustained (increased cardiac contractility). Extra note: this will also disrupt the H+/K+ pump in the stomach (you will learn more about this in GI). [NOTES] mhayajne@student.touro.edu
ConceptDigoxin: Na+/K+ ATPase block → ↑Na+ → ↓ NCX activity → ↑ intracellular Ca2+

Questions 6 and 7 An electrocardiogram (ECG) on a person shows ventricular extrasystoles. The extrasystolic beat would produce
  1. A. increased pulse pressure because contractility is increased
  2. B. increased pulse pressure because heart rate is increased
  3. C. decreased pulse pressure because ventricular filling time is increased

  5. E. decreased pulse pressure because the PR interval is increased
AnswerD. decreased pulse pressure because stroke volume is decreased
Explanation from the source
The answer is D [V G]. On the extrasystolic beat, pulse pressure decreases because there is inadequate ventricular filling time—the ventricle beats “too soon.” As a result, stroke volume decreases.

  1. A. increased pulse pressure because the contractility of the ventricle is increased
  2. B. increased pulse pressure because total peripheral resistance (TPR) is decreased

A 55-year-old man with long-standing hypertension is prescribed a medication that blocks β-adrenergic receptors. Which of the following physiologic effects would most likely be reduced by this therapy?
  1. A) Relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle mediated by β₂-adrenergic receptors
  2. B) Contraction of vascular smooth muscle mediated by α₁-adrenergic receptors
  3. C) Increased release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of cardiac muscle via β₁-adrenergic receptors
  4. D) Vasodilation of skeletal muscle arterioles mediated by muscarinic receptors
AnswerC. Increased release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of cardiac muscle via β₁-adrenergic receptors
WhyCardiac β1 stimulation raises cAMP so protein kinase A phosphorylates L-type Ca²⁺ channels and phospholamban, increasing SR Ca²⁺ release and contractility, which a β-blocker reduces.
Explanation from the source
Epinephrine binds β-adrenergic receptors (Gs-coupled). β₁ in the heart: ↑ cAMP → ↑ Ca²⁺ influx → stronger cardiac muscle contraction. β₂ in lungs/intestine: relaxation of smooth muscle. β-blockers antagonize these receptors, reducing heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure → basis of their antihypertensive use. α₁-mediated vasoconstriction and muscarinic vasodilation are not blocked by β-blockers.
Conceptβ-blocker reduces β1-mediated ↑ SR Ca2+ release in cardiac muscle

8. A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute heart failure. The patient requires immediate drug therapy to improve his cardiac function. Which one of the following drugs would be most beneficial?
  1. A. Phenylephrine.
  2. B. Epinephrine.
  3. C. Norepinephrine.
  4. D. Albuterol.
  5. E. Dobutamine.
AnswerE. Dobutamine.
Explanation from the source
Rationale: Dobutamine increases cardiac output without significantly increasing heart rate, a complicating condition in heart failure. Because epinephrine can significantly increase heart rate, it is not typically used for acute heart failure. Both norepinephrine and phenylephrine have significant α1-receptor-stimulating properties. The subsequent increase in blood pressure would worsen the heart failure. Albuterol, a ß 2-selective-receptor agonist, would not significantly improve contractility of the heart.
ConceptAcute heart failure drug therapy → dobutamine

Describe what would happen to Stroke Volume in the following situations (increase or decrease). 1) Increase in Preload = ________ in Stroke Volume
Answerincrease
WhyGreater preload (EDV) stretches sarcomeres toward optimal length, so by the Frank–Starling mechanism the ventricle ejects a larger stroke volume.
Explanation from the source
Preload is the amount of volume in the left ventricle. The more you have the more volume you can eject during systole. Afterload is the same as aortic pressure. The greater the aortic pressure/afterload, the harder it is for the left ventricle to pump the blood out -> decrease in SV. Increase in contractility will increase stroke volume. The stronger the contraction = the more blood you can eject from left ventricle.
Concept↑ Preload → ↑ stroke volume

Which of the following is an effect of sympathetic stimulation?
Show figure
  1. A. Phosphorylation of phospholamban and increased calcium pumped into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
  2. B. Phosphorylation of phospholamban and decreased calcium pumped into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
  3. C. Beta 2-mediated increase in contractility
  4. D. Alpha 1-mediated increase in contractility
  5. E. Beta 1 decreases in cAMP and increased contractility
AnswerA. Phosphorylation of phospholamban and increased calcium pumped into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
WhySympathetic β1 stimulation raises cAMP, and protein kinase A phosphorylates phospholamban, releasing its inhibition of SERCA so more Ca²⁺ is pumped into the SR, speeding relaxation and enlarging the next release.
Explanation from the source
All heart effects for SNS stimulation are going to be mediated through B1 receptors. The effect there is to increase cAMP production. Increased cAMP activates PKA which can phosphorylate target proteins including phospholamban. Phosphorylation of this target causes an INCREASE in the rate of calcium reuptake into the SR. This allows for quicker repolarization as well as creating a greater concentration gradient for subsequent depolarization. PP-1: phosphatase (which dephosphorylate proteins when not phosphorylated themselves). Active PKA phosphorylates phospholamban (PLB; increases SERCA activity) and PP-1 (prevents dephosphorylation of PLB by PP-1)
ConceptSympathetic: phospholamban phosphorylation → ↑ Ca2+ pumped into SR

Activation of Na/K ATPase pumps: Would decrease intracellular Ca2+ Antagonization of postsynaptic Beta-1 receptors: Would decrease contractility Intracellular calcium is directly related with cardiac contractility. Which of the following best describes the process of calcium handling during cardiac muscle contraction?
  1. a. Following depolarization, calcium enters the myocardial cells through ryanodine receptors, which then triggers more calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  2. b. Following depolarization, calcium enters the myocardial cells through dihydropyridine receptors, which then triggers the release of additional calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via ryanodine receptors.
  3. c. Calcium is released directly from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during depolarization, bypassing any extracellular calcium influx.
  4. d.) The magnitude of tension in myocardial cells is independent of calcium levels inside the cell.
Answerb. Following depolarization, calcium enters the myocardial cells through dihydropyridine receptors, which then triggers the release of additional calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via ryanodine receptors.
WhyDepolarization opens L-type Ca²⁺ channels (dihydropyridine receptors) in the T-tubules, and this trigger Ca²⁺ opens ryanodine receptors to release far more Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Explanation from the source
Action Potential arrives to myocardial cell Ca2+ channels on cell membrane open (dihydropyridine receptors) Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum (ryanodine receptors) Ca2+ binds to Troponin C moving tropomyosin out of the way for muscle contraction Relaxation occurs by sarcoplasmic reticulum collecting Ca2+ in cytosol via Ca2+ ATPase and expulsion from the cell via Ca2+-Na+ exchanger
ConceptCardiac Ca2+ handling: DHP-receptor entry triggers SR release via ryanodine receptors

Which of the following statements best describes the mechanism by which the sympathetic nervous system increases cardiac contractility?
  1. a. Phosphorylation of phospholamban stimulates the Ca²⁺ ATPase, resulting in greater uptake and storage of Ca²⁺ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum, enhancing contractility.
  2. b. Activation of muscarinic receptors increases the inward Ca²⁺ current during the plateau phase of the action potential, leading to stronger contraction.
  3. c. The effects of the sympathetic nervous system result in a prolonged contraction due to decreased Ca²⁺uptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  4. d. Sympathetic receptors are coupled via Gi protein, which decreases cAMP levels and reduces contractility.
Answera. Phosphorylation of phospholamban stimulates the Ca²⁺ ATPase, resulting in greater uptake and storage of Ca²⁺ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum, enhancing contractility.

This allows SERCA to pump more calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) after contraction.   • SGA Drive › Physiology I 2024 (Harlem resources) › Physio Exam 2: Cardio › Physio Exam 2_ Cardio › TA Exam Reviews › 2024 Physio I Exam 2 TA Review- Montana.pptx · 46: B (B) end-systolic volume

Correct key: (B) end-systolic volume. EF = SV/EDV; a higher EF means more of the EDV is ejected, so ESV falls. CO, SV, pulse pressure and systolic pressure rise. The Montana 2024 TA Review and BRS textbook keys (B) are right; the BRS Test 2 pptx key (C, heart rate) is wrong.
WhyEF = SV/EDV, so a higher ejection fraction ejects more of the EDV and leaves less behind: end-systolic volume (EDV − SV) falls.
Explanation from the source
An increase in ejection fraction means that a higher fraction of the end-diastolic volume is ejected in the stroke volume. When this situation occurs, the volume remaining in the ventricle after systole, the end-systolic volume, will be reduced. Cardiac output, pulse pressure, stroke volume, and systolic pressure will be increased.
Concept↑ Ejection fraction → ↓ end-systolic volume

An increase in contractility produces an increase in cardiac output for a given end-diastolic volume, or pressure. The Frank–Starling relationship demonstrates the matching of cardiac output (what leaves the heart) with venous return (what returns to the heart). An increase in contractility (positive inotropic effect) will shift the curve upward.
Concept↑ Contractility on Frank–Starling diagram = ↑ CO for a given EDV

Which one of the following is the best index of preload?
  1. A. Blood volume
  2. B. Central venous pressure
  3. C. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
  4. D. Left ventricular end-diastolic volume
  5. E. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure
AnswerD. Left ventricular end-diastolic volume
WhyPreload is the sarcomere length at end-diastole, and the measure most directly tied to that stretch is left ventricular end-diastolic volume; pressures and blood volume act only through it.
Explanation from the source
The answer is d. (Berne, 3/e, pp 202-206.) Preload is defined as the sarcomere length at the end of diastole. The parameter most directly related to sarcomere length during this time period is left ventricular end-diastolic volume. Although blood volume, central venous pressure, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, and left ventricular end-diastolic pressure can all influence preload, they all exert their influence through changes in enddiastolic volume. Each of these parameters could change without altering preload.
ConceptBest index of preload: LV end-diastolic volume

Which one of the following is the best index of afterload?
  1. A. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure
  2. B. Left ventricular mean systolic pressure
  3. C. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
  4. D. Total peripheral resistance
  5. E. Mean arterial blood pressure
AnswerB. Left ventricular mean systolic pressure
WhyAfterload is the wall stress the ventricle must overcome to eject, which by Laplace is proportional to ventricular pressure × radius, so mean LV systolic pressure indexes it best.
Explanation from the source
The answer is b. (Berne, 3/e, pp 204-206.) The afterload is the force that the sarcomeres must overcome in order to shorten during systole. According to the law of Laplace, this force is proportional to the pressure (P) and radius (r) of the ventricle during ejection (force «< P Xr). The mean left ventricular systolic pressure would therefore be the best index of afterload. Although total peripheral resistance can influence afterload by causing changes in mean arterial blood pressure, these factors can only influence afterload by causing a change in ventricular pressure. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and left ventricular end-diastolic pressure are estimates of the volume of blood in the ventricle during diastole and are indices of preload.
ConceptBest index of afterload: LV mean systolic pressure

Stroke volume is increased by
  1. A. A decrease in venous compliance
  2. B. An increase in afterload
  3. C. A decrease in contractility
  4. D. An increase in heart rate
  5. E. A decrease in coronary blood flow
AnswerA decrease in venous compliance
WhyLower venous compliance shifts blood from unstressed to stressed volume, raising venous return and preload, so the Frank–Starling mechanism increases stroke volume.
Explanation from the source
The answer is a. (Rhoades, pp 263-269.) Stroke volume depends on preload, afterload, and contractility. Decreasing venous compliance forces more blood into the ventricle, resulting in an increased preload and an increased stroke volume. Increasing afterload and decreasing contractility decreases stroke volume. An increase in heart rate may result in a decreased filling time and, therefore, a decrease in preload and stroke volume. A decrease in coronary blood flow causes a decrease in ventricular contractility and stroke volume.
ConceptSV ↑ by ↓ venous compliance (more venous return/preload)

F f from the administration of a positive inotropic drug such as digoxin will An Increase In card lac allow the heart to produce the same force at a lower volume and thus elimexcitabi | ity inate the need for an increase in volume of fluid.

  1. A. Increasing ventricular contractility

Explanation from the source
The answer is b. (Rhoades, pp 268-269.) Stroke volume is determined by preload, afterload, and contractility. An ectopic extrasystole caused by a ventricular focus is characterized by
  1. A. Interruption of the regular SA node discharge
  2. B. Retrograde conduction of the action potential to the atria
  3. C. A skipped ventricular contraction
  4. D. A skipped atrial contraction
  5. E. A larger than normal force of contraction
AnswerC. A skipped ventricular contraction
WhyA premature ventricular beat leaves the ventricles refractory when the next SA impulse arrives, so that normal beat produces no ventricular contraction, giving a compensatory pause.
Explanation from the source
The answer is c. (Guyton, pp 98, 136-138.) A premature heartbeat, or . ectopic extrasystole, places the myocardium in a refractory period at the contraction time of arrival of the next normal stimulus from the SA node. Therefore, no A | th ventricular contraction can occur. The impulse from the ectopic focus is arger than incapable of exciting the bundle of His and thus no retrograde conduction normal force of to the atrium takes place. Inasmuch as the ectopic event does not extend to . the atrium, the atrium continues to contract regularly under the influence contraction of the SA node. The ventricular contraction is smaller because the heart has not filled to its normal end-diastolic volume when the extrasystole occurs. In addition, the extrasystole does not propagate normally through the ventricle, so the force of contraction is reduced.
ConceptVentricular ectopic extrasystole → skipped ventricular contraction

  1. A. Decreasing ventricular compliance
  2. B. Increasing venous compliance
  3. C. Decreasing total peripheral resistance
  4. D. Increasing heart rate
  5. E. Decreasing atrial contractility
AnswerC. Decreasing total peripheral resistance
WhyLower total peripheral resistance reduces aortic pressure and thus afterload, so the ventricle ejects more blood and stroke volume rises.
Explanation from the source
The answer is c. (Guyton, pp 211-213, 976.) Soke volume is influenced by ventricular preload, afterload, and contractility. Decreasing total peripheral resistance may result in a decrease in afterload and therefore an increase in stroke volume. Decreasing ventricular compliance (making the heart stiffer) or increasing venous compliance will decrease ventricular filling and, therefore, preload and stroke volume. Similarly, increasing heart rate and deceasing atrial contractility will decrease filling and stroke volume
ConceptSV ↑ by ↓ total peripheral resistance (↓ afterload)

Which of the following agents or changes has a negative inotropic effect on the heart?
  1. (A) Increased heart rate
  2. (B) Sympathetic stimulation
  3. (C) Norepinephrine
  4. (D) Acetylcholine (ACh)
  5. (E) Cardiac glycosides
AnswerD. Acetylcholine (ACh)
WhyAcetylcholine acts on M2 receptors (Gi, ↓cAMP) to reduce Ca²⁺ entry, giving a negative inotropic effect, mainly in the atria.
Explanation from the source
A negative inotropic effect is one that decreases myocardial contractility. Contractility is the ability to develop tension at a fixed muscle length. Factors that decrease contractility are those that decrease the intracellular2+ ]. Increasing heart rate increases intracellular Ca2+ ] because more Ca2+ ions enter the cell during the plateau of each action potential. Sympathetic stimulation and norepinephrine increase intracellular Ca2+ ] by increasing entry during the plateau and increasing the storage of Ca2+ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) . Cardiac glycosides increase intracellular Ca2+ ] by inhibiting the Na+ –K+ pump, thereby inhibiting Na+– Ca2+ exchange (a mechanism that pumps Ca2+ out of the cell). Acetylcholine (ACh) has a negative inotropic effect on the atria.
ConceptNegative inotropic agent: acetylcholine

Which of the following statements about cardiac muscle is most accurate?

  3. C) In cardiac muscle the initiation of the action potential causes an immediate opening of slow calcium channels
  4. D) Cardiac muscle repolarization is caused by opening of sodium channels
  5. E) Mucopolysaccharides inside the T-tubules bind chloride ions
AnswerB. The strength and contraction of cardiac muscle depends on the amount of calcium surrounding cardiac myocytes
WhyCardiac contraction depends on extracellular Ca²⁺ entering through L-type channels during the plateau, which triggers calcium-induced calcium release, so contraction strength tracks the Ca²⁺ around the myocytes.

Explanation The cardiac muscle stores much more calcium in its tubular system than skeletal muscle and is much more dependent on extracellular calcium than the skeletal muscle. At the initiation of the action potential, the fast sodium channels open first, followed later by the opening of the slow calcium channels.

803Borderline
Match the following: 1. Composed of actin, tropomyosin, and troponin 2. Contains the myosin-binding site 3. Invaginate at the Z lines, continuous with the cell membrane, and carry APs to the inside of the cell 4. Composed of myosin 5. Functions to block the myosin-binding site 6. Upon binding to Ca2+, causes a conformational change that allows for actin-myosin interaction 7. Site of storage and release of Ca2+ for excitation-contraction coupling
  1. A. Transverse (T) tubules
  2. B. Thin filaments
  3. C. Sarcoplasmic Reticulum
  4. D. Thick filaments
  5. E. Actin
  6. F. Troponin C
  7. G. Tropomyosin
Answer1-B, 2-E, 3-A, 4-D, 5-G, 6-F, 7-C. 1. Composed of actin, tropomyosin, and troponin → B) thin filaments 2. Contains the myosin-binding site → E) Actin 3. Invaginate at the Z lines, continuous with the cell membrane, and carry APs to the inside of the cell → A) Transverse (T) tubules 4. Composed of myosin → D) thick filaments 5. Functions to block the myosin-binding site → G) tropomyosin 6. Upon binding to Ca2+, causes a conformational change that allows for actin-myosin interaction → F) troponin C 7. Site of storage and release of Ca2+ for excitation-contraction coupling → C) Sarcoplasmic Reticulum
WhyThin filaments (actin with its myosin-binding sites, tropomyosin, troponin) and thick filaments (myosin) form the sarcomere; T tubules carry the AP inward, the SR stores and releases Ca²⁺, and Ca²⁺ binding troponin C shifts tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites.
sarcomere/T-tubule/SR basics are MSK I muscle content; only the Ca2+-troponin C / SR-release items are in the L22 excitation-contraction sequence

A 62-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension arrives in the emergency room with substernal chest pain for the last hour. He is given intravenous nitroglycerin to help reduce the pain. Which of the following would be expected with the use of this drug?
  1. a. Arterial blood pressure is increased.

  5. e. Venous return to the heart is increased.
AnswerD. d. Myocardial oxygen demand is decreased.
WhyNitroglycerin venodilates, lowering venous return and preload, which shrinks ventricular radius and wall stress (Laplace) and so decreases myocardial O₂ demand.
Explanation from the source
Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator = decreases preload Nitrates are commonly used for the treatment of angina and coronary artery disease.Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator because it releases nitric oxide in smooth muscle causing an increase in cyclic GMP and vascular smooth muscle relaxation. Nitroglycerin dilates the coronary arteries, thereby increasing coronary blood flow
ConceptNitroglycerin (venodilator) in angina → ↓ myocardial O2 demand

Law of LaPlace, what is the equation?

Law of LaPlace, what is the equation? What is its function/Why does it relate to the heart?

WhyBy Laplace (P = 2HT/r), generating higher pressure requires a thicker wall, so the LV, which pumps against systemic pressure, has a thicker wall than the RV.
ConceptLaw of Laplace: P ∝ wall thickness × tension / radius; why LV wall is thicker than RV

AnswerHow to solve: CO= 250 / (0.2-0.15) = 250 / 0.05 = 5000 mL/min
WhyBy the Fick principle, CO = O2 consumption / (arterial − venous O2 content) = 250 mL/min ÷ (0.20 − 0.15 mL O2/mL) = 250/0.05 = 5000 mL/min.
Explanation from the source

On the following slides you will see a set of two PV loops. Identify the physiological change/stress that is indicated overall. For the PV loops on the left, identify the changes that occur with a single cardiac cycle in response to the physiological change relative to the control loop (black). For the PV loops on the right, identify what has changed after 20 cardiac cycles relative to the change after a single cardiac cycle Unknown 1. Have the parameters below ↑, ↓ or ↔ when comparing the blue loop to the control loop? [table: Preload | Afterload | Contractility] Have the parameters below ↑, ↓ or ↔ when comparing the blue loop to the red loop? Discuss why these changes occur. [table: Stroke volume | Ejection fraction]
AnswerUnknown 1 – Increased Afterload. Blue vs control: Preload ↔; Afterload ↑; Contractility ↔. Blue vs red loop: Stroke volume ↑; Ejection fraction ↑. (Red loop labels: ↑Afterload (primary); ↑ Preload (secondary))
WhyIncreased afterload makes the aortic valve open at higher pressure, so the first beat ejects less and leaves a bigger ESV; that residual volume raises EDV over later beats and Frank–Starling restores SV and EF.
Explanation from the source
Figure on left/AFTER 1 CARDIAC CYCLE COMPARED TO CONTROL: Preload, unchanged (no change in EDV); Afterload, increased (aortic valve clearly opening at higher LV pressure, and closing at higher LV pressure). An example would be increased aortic blood pressure. Contractility, no change (ESPVR has not changed [slope]) Figure on right/AFTER 20 CARDIAC CYCLES COMPARD TO AFTER 1 CARDIAC CYCLE: Preload, after the initial acute increase in afterload, there was a decrease in stroke volume (width of blue loop) and an increase in ESV. Thus, continued/normal venous return on top of an increased ESV will lead to a secondary increase in EDV (aka: preload). Afterload, the afterload remains at its acutely increased level Stroke volume, increased due to increased afterload (frank-starling). This helps compensate for the acutely reduced stroke volume observed in the blue loop on left. Ejection fraction, the frank starling mechanism of heart (length-tension relationship at onset of ventricular systole) will increase the ejection fraction. This is NOT due to a change in inotropy (as you ESPVR has note changed)
ConceptPV loops ↑ afterload: acute change and after 20 cycles (SV, EF recover)

On the following slides you will see a set of two PV loops. Identify the physiological change/stress that is indicated overall. For the PV loops on the left, identify the changes that occur with a single cardiac cycle in response to the physiological change relative to the control loop (black). For the PV loops on the right, identify what has changed after 20 cardiac cycles relative to the change after a single cardiac cycle Unknown 2. Have the parameters below ↑, ↓ or ↔ when comparing the blue loop to the control loop? [table: Preload | Afterload | Contractility] Have the parameters in the adjacent table ↑, ↓ or ↔ when comparing the blue loop to the red loop? Discuss why these changes occur. [table: Stroke volume | Ejection fraction | Systolic arterial pressure | Diastolic arterial pressure]
AnswerUnknown 2 – Increased Preload. Blue vs control: Preload ↑; Afterload ↔; Contractility ↔. Blue vs red loop: Stroke volume ↓; Ejection fraction ↓; Systolic arterial pressure ↑; Diastolic arterial pressure ↑. (Red loop labels: ↑ Afterload (secondary); ↑ Preload (primary))
WhyIncreased preload raises EDV and, through Frank–Starling, SV at unchanged contractility; the larger SV then raises arterial pressure, a secondary afterload rise that trims SV and EF somewhat over later beats.
Explanation from the source
Figure on left/AFTER 1 CARDIAC CYCLE COMPARED TO CONTROL: Preload, increased EDV (preload), thus increased stretch of myocytes. Afterload, no change in afterload as you see LV volume start to decrease (ejection) at the same pressure in the blue loop and the black loop Contractility, no change as the ESPVR has not changed (slope). What has changed is the marked increase in preload which leads to increased stroke volume due to frank starling mechanism (NOT inotropy/contractility which is characterized by ESPVR). Figure on right/AFTER 20 CARDIAC CYCLES COMPARD TO AFTER 1 CARDIAC CYCLE: assume that HR is unchanged. Preload, increased in the same fashion as we saw with blue loop. This is the primary/initial change and persists Afterload, afterload has increased secondary to the increased preload. Why? There is more volume being pumped into the system. More volume leads to more pressure. Contractility, still no change (ESPVR has not changed) Stroke volume, compared to the blue loop, stroke volume has DECREASED. This is due to the fact that there is now a secondary increase in afterload (thus, the aortic valve will close earlier). Compared to control, still increased Ejection fraction, compared to the blue loop, ejection fraction has DECREASED. This is again due to the secondary increase in afterload (not preload since it is the same). Compared to control, still increased. Systolic arterial pressure, increased…this is the illustration of the secondary increase in afterload Diastolic arterial pressure, increase…again, the illustration of the secondary increase in afterload due to a greater volume of blood in the arterial system.
ConceptPV loops ↑ preload: acute change and after 20 cycles (SV, EF, arterial pressures)

For the PV loops on the left, identify the changes that occur with a single cardiac cycle in response to the physiological change relative to the control loop (black). For the PV loops on the right, identify what has changed after 20 cardiac cycles relative to the change after a single cardiac cycle Unknown 3. Have the parameters below ↑, ↓ or ↔ when comparing the blue loop to the control loop? [table: Preload | Afterload | Contractility] Have the parameters in the adjacent table ↑, ↓ or ↔ when comparing the blue loop to the red loop? Discuss why these changes occur. [table: Stroke volume | Ejection fraction | End-systolic volume | End-diastolic volume]
AnswerUnknown 3 – Increased Contractility. Blue vs control: Preload ↔; Afterload ↔; Contractility ↑. Blue vs red loop: Stroke volume ↓; Ejection fraction ↔/↓; End-systolic volume ↑; End-diastolic volume ↓. (Red loop labels: ↑Inotropy (primary); ↑Afterload (secondary); ↓Preload (secondary))

Explanation from the source
Figure on left/AFTER 1 CARDIAC CYCLE COMPARED TO CONTROL: Preload, EDV is unchanged. Thus, no change in preload Afterload, no change in afterload as you see LV volume start to decrease (ejection) at the same pressure in the blue loop and the black loop Contractility, ESPVR has changed! What does this mean. The SLOPE of the ESPVR line has INCREASED which indicates an INCREASED CONTRACTILITY. Now, the increased stroke volume that you see is due to inotropy (NOT frank starling) Figure on right/AFTER 20 CARDIAC CYCLES COMPARD TO AFTER 1 CARDIAC CYCLE: assume that HR is unchanged. Preload, after the initial acute increase in contractility, there was an increase in stroke volume (width of blue loop) and decrease in ESV. Thus, continued/normal venous return on top of an decreased ESV will lead to a secondary decrease in EDV (aka: preload). Afterload, afterload has increased secondary to the increased contractility/inotropy. Why? There is more volume being pumped into the system. More volume leads to more pressure. Contractility, the same slope of the ESPVR line will be observed…increased contractility. Stroke volume, compared to the blue loop, stroke volume has DECREASED. This is due to the fact that there is now a secondary increase in afterload (thus, the aortic valve will close earlier) AND a secondary decrease in preload. Compared to control, still increased Ejection fraction, compared to the blue loop, ejection fraction has likely DECREASED. This is again due to the secondary increase in afterload and secondary decrease in preload. Compared to control, still increased. Systolic arterial pressure, increased…this is the illustration of the secondary increase in afterload Diastolic arterial pressure, increase…again, the illustration of the secondary increase in afterload due to a greater volume of blood in the arterial system. End systolic volume, compared to the blue loop, ESV has increased. This is due to the secondary increase in afterload and the secondary decrease in preload End diastolic volume, compared to the blue loop, EDV has decreased. See notes for preload above. Can think of as secondary decrease in preload being due to increased stroke volume with primary increase in inotropy.
ConceptPV loops ↑ contractility: acute change and after 20 cycles (SV, EF, ESV, EDV)

[table: Contractility | Stroke volume | End-diastolic volume | End-systolic volume | Ejection fraction]
AnswerUnknown 4 – Systolic Heart Failure. Contractility ↓; Stroke volume ↓; End-diastolic volume ↑; End-systolic volume ↑; Ejection fraction ↓
WhySystolic heart failure flattens the ESPVR (↓contractility), so ESV rises and SV falls; residual volume plus normal venous return raises EDV, but less than ESV, so EF falls.
Explanation from the source
Systolic failure is defined as impaired ventricular contractility • Impaired contractility causes ESV volume to increase • EDV increases because increased ESV is added to normal venous return (Frank Starling) • The increase in EDV is not at great as the increase in ESV • Ejection fraction decreases • Increased diastolic volume can cause increased LV and LA pressure. Wall Stress (σ) = pressure x radius / 2 x wall thickness
ConceptPV loop of systolic heart failure: ↓ contractility, ↓ SV, ↑ EDV, ↑ ESV, ↓ EF

The following slides demonstrate PV loops after many many cardiac cycles associated with cardiovascular pathology. Please identify the changes relative to control (black loop) and the condition that is likely illustrated Unknown 5. Have the parameters below ↑, ↓ or ↔ when comparing the red loop to the control loop? Discuss why these changes occur. [table: Contractility | Stroke volume | End-diastolic volume | End-systolic volume | Ejection fraction]
AnswerUnknown 5 – Diastolic Heart Failure. Contractility ↔; Stroke volume ↓; End-diastolic volume ↓; End-systolic volume ↔; Ejection fraction ↔/↓
WhyDiastolic heart failure is a stiff, poorly compliant ventricle (steeper EDPVR), so it fills to a smaller EDV at a higher filling pressure; SV falls while contractility and ESV are unchanged.
Explanation from the source
Diastolic failure is defined as impaired ventricular filling. • ↓ ventricular compliance is caused either by ventricular hypertrophy or ↓ lusitropy • Ventricular filling pressure ↑ →→ ↓ ventricular filling and ↑ LVEDP • LV → Increased LA and pulmonary venous pressure → pulmonary congestion • RV → Increased RA pressure and systemic venous pressure → peripheral edema • Ejection fraction may or may not change. Graph callouts: Low ventricular compliance = low end-diastolic volume; Low ventricular compliance = higher filling pressure.
ConceptPV loop of diastolic heart failure: ↓ EDV, ↓ SV, ESV and contractility unchanged

841
Each of the following slides are titled with different cardiovascular conditions. Please draw (superimposed on normal loop) the loop you are likely to observe with the indicated condition. You can presume that the condition has not yet led to marked remodeling of the left ventricle. Acute Mitral Stenosis
AnswerDecrease in EDV (preload) due to impaired left ventricular filling Decreased stroke volume by Frank-Starling mechanism
WhyMitral stenosis impedes flow from the left atrium into the LV, so EDV (preload) falls and, by Frank–Starling, stroke volume falls.
Explanation from the source
What condition is this? Mitral valve stenosis. What does it cause? pressure difference between left atria and left ventricle during ventricular diastole. What happens to P-V loop as a result? LVEDV: a stenotic mitral valve will hinder ventricular filling from the left atria to the left ventricle. Thus, you should expect a decrease in LVEDV. LVESV: a stenotic mitral valve will NOT hinder ventricular outflow to the aorta, nor is there a concern with backflow. HOWEVER, with reduced LVEDV volume, the stretch of the myocytes will be reduced. This will decrease contraction magnitude (actin/myosin overlap) and stroke volume. Thus, I’d expect to see a smaller stroke volume. Stroke volume: see LVESV Cardiac output: cardiac output is HRxSV. If stroke volume is decreased, will HR “pick up the slack”. Yes, but it cannot pick up all of the slack or doesn’t in an acute example. As a result, CO will be lower. Systolic aortic pressure: As noted above, contraction, stroke volume and cardiac output are all decreased. With less outflow and contraction, there will be a decrease in systolic aortic pressure.
ConceptDraw PV loop in acute mitral stenosis: ↓ EDV (preload) → ↓ SV
Slides
842
Each of the following slides are titled with different cardiovascular conditions. Please draw (superimposed on normal loop) the loop you are likely to observe with the indicated condition. You can presume that the condition has not yet led to marked remodeling of the left ventricle. Acute Mitral Regurgitation
AnswerBlood ejected into both aorta and left atrium upon ventricular contraction (systole) Reduced afterload→ lower end-systolic volume Elevated left atrial pressure is transmitted to left ventricle during filling causing an increase in LVEDV and LVEDP Stroke volume is increased
WhyIn acute mitral regurgitation the LV ejects into both the aorta and the low-pressure left atrium, so effective afterload falls and ESV drops, while the high left atrial pressure raises EDV, so total SV rises.
Explanation from the source
What condition is this? Mitral valve insufficiency What does it cause? Backflow of blood into left atria during ventricular systole reduces ventricular “efficiency”. That is, during contraction, some blood leaks back from LV to LA. What happens to P-V loop as a result? LVEDV: regurgitation at the mitral valve should have little impact on inflow into the left ventricle. HOWEVER, regurgitation during systole means that atrial volume and pressure will be higher than normal. Thus, filling pressure and “available volume” during ventricular diastole will be higher and result in much greater LVEDVs. This is the ventricle accommodating the needs of the LA (note: pulmonary pressures will also rise to keep blood moving forward). LVESV: The LV is again accommodating/compensating for the increased volume and will, by Frank Starling definition), increase contraction in an effort to get to normal LVESV values. In addition, the regurgitation through the mitral valve allows blood to outflow into the left atria (in addition to the aorta). Thus, SV will be high and LVESV will be near normal (maybe slightly reduced) due to extra “escape” into LA. Stroke volume: see LVESV. Will be greatly increased…(although not all of this stroke volume goes to aorta, some is going to left atria. Thus, the contribution of stroke volume to effective cardiac output is reduced). Cardiac output: cardiac output is HRxSV. Here, stroke volume is increased….although, not all of it is going to the periphery (into aorta). However, by definition, cardiac output will be increased as a compensatory mechanism. Systolic aortic pressure: since some volume and pressure can escape backwards into the LA, LV pressure will not increase as high. In sum, you end up with a reduced systolic aortic blood pressure.
ConceptDraw PV loop in acute mitral regurgitation: ↓ ESV, ↑ EDV, ↑ total SV

Questions 9–12 If the heart rate is 70 beats/min, then the cardiac output of this ventricle is closest to
  1. A. 3.45 L/min
  2. B. 4.55 L/min
  3. C. 5.25 L/min
  4. D. 8.00 L/min
  5. E. 9.85 L/min
AnswerC. 5.25 L/min
Explanation from the source
The answer is C [IV E 1, G 1, 2]. Stroke volume is the volume ejected from the ventricle and is represented on the pressure–volume loop as phase 2 → 3; end-diastolic volume is about 140 mL and end-systolic volume is about 65 mL; the difference, or stroke volume, is 75 mL. Cardiac output is calculated as stroke volume × heart rate or 75 mL × 70 beats/min = 5250 mL/min or 5.25 L/min.

Questions 25 and 26 Curve A in the figure represents
  1. A. aortic pressure
  2. B. ventricular pressure
  3. C. atrial pressure
  4. D. ventricular volume

WhyCurve A is aortic pressure: it rises steeply after the QRS as the ventricle ejects, then falls with runoff, showing the dicrotic notch when the aortic valve closes.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A [V A to G]. The electrocardiogram (ECG) tracing serves as a reference. The QRS complex marks ventricular depolarization, followed immediately by ventricular contraction. Aortic pressure increases steeply after QRS, as blood is ejected from the ventricles. After reaching peak pressure, aortic pressure decreases as blood runs off into the arteries. The characteristic dicrotic notch (“blip” in the aortic pressure curve) appears when the aortic valve closes. Aortic pressure continues to decrease as blood flows out of the aorta.

  4. D. ventricular volume

WhyCurve B is ventricular volume: it rises slightly with atrial systole, stays constant during isovolumetric contraction, drops during ejection after the QRS, then refills in diastole.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D [V A to G]. Ventricular volume increases slightly with atrial systole (P wave), is constant during isovolumetric contraction (QRS), and then decreases dramatically after the QRS, when blood is ejected from the ventricle.
ConceptWiggers-type traces: curve B = ventricular volume

The following measurements were obtained in a male patient: Central venous pressure: 10 mm Hg Heart rate: 70 beats/min Systemic arterial [O2] = 0.24 mL O2/mL Mixed venous [O2] = 0.16 mL O2/mL Whole body O2 consumption: 500 mL/min What is this patient’s cardiac output?
  1. A. 1.65 L/min
  2. B. 4.55 L/min
  3. C. 5.00 L/min
  4. D. 6.25 L/min
  5. E. 8.00 L/min
AnswerD. 6.25 L/min
WhyBy the Fick principle, CO = O2 consumption ÷ (arterial − venous O2 content) = 500 mL/min ÷ (0.24 − 0.16 mL O2/mL) = 6.25 L/min.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D [IV J]. Cardiac output is calculated by the Fick principle if whole body oxygen (O2) consumption and [O2] in the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein are measured. Mixed venous blood could substitute for a pulmonary artery sample, and peripheral arterial blood could substitute for a pulmonary vein sample. Central venous pressure and heart rate are not needed for this calculation. [equation printed as a picture on p.210, transcribed: Cardiac output = 500 mL/min / (0.24 mL O2/mL − 0.16 mL O2/mL) = 6250 mL/min, or 6.25 L/min]
ConceptFick principle: CO = VO2 / (arterial − venous O2 content)

If heart rate increases, which phase of the cardiac cycle is decreased?
  1. A. Atrial systole
  2. B. Isovolumetric ventricular contraction
  3. C. Rapid ventricular ejection
  4. D. Reduced ventricular ejection
  5. E. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation
  6. F. Rapid ventricular filling
  7. G. Reduced ventricular filling
AnswerG. Reduced ventricular filling
WhyA faster heart rate shortens diastole mostly by cutting reduced ventricular filling (diastasis), the late, slow-filling phase, while systole changes little.
Explanation from the source
The answer is G [Chapter 3, V; Figure 3.15]. When heart rate increases, the time between ventricular contractions (for refilling of the ventricles with blood) decreases. Because most ventricular filling occurs during the “reduced” phase, this phase is the most compromised by an increase in heart rate.
Concept↑ Heart rate shortens reduced ventricular filling (diastasis) most

Which phase of the cardiac cycle is absent if there is no P wave on the electrocardiogram (ECG)?
  1. A. Atrial systole
  2. B. Isovolumetric ventricular contraction
  3. C. Rapid ventricular ejection
  4. D. Reduced ventricular ejection
  5. E. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation
  6. F. Rapid ventricular filling
  7. G. Reduced ventricular filling
AnswerA. Atrial systole
WhyThe P wave is atrial depolarization, so without it the atria never contract and atrial systole (the atrial kick) is absent.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A [Chapter 3, V; Figure 3.15]. The P wave represents electrical activation (depolarization) of the atria. Atrial contraction is always preceded by electrical activation.
ConceptNo P wave on ECG → atrial systole absent

The following diagram applies to Questions 66 and 67 During which labeled wave or segment of the electrocardiogram (ECG) is aortic pressure at its lowest value?

  4. D. D
  5. E. E
AnswerC. C
WhyAortic pressure falls throughout diastole as blood runs off, so it is lowest at the QRS (C), just before the ventricle ejects and the aortic valve opens.

The answer is C [Chapter 3, V; Figure 3.15]. Aortic pressure is lowest just before the ventricles contract.

During which phase of the cardiac cycle does ventricular pressure rise but ventricular volume remain constant?
  1. A. Atrial systole
  2. B. Isovolumetric ventricular contraction
  3. C. Rapid ventricular ejection
  4. D. Reduced ventricular ejection
  5. E. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation
  6. F. Rapid ventricular filling
  7. G. Reduced ventricular filling
AnswerB. Isovolumetric ventricular contraction
WhyDuring isovolumetric contraction the ventricle contracts with both mitral and aortic valves closed, so pressure rises steeply while volume stays at EDV until the aortic valve opens.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B [Chapter 3, V; Figure 3.15]. Because the ventricles are contracting during isovolumetric contraction, ventricular pressure increases. Because all of the valves are closed, the contraction is isovolumetric. No blood is ejected into the aorta until ventricular pressure increases enough to open the aortic valve.
ConceptVentricular pressure rises at constant volume = isovolumetric contraction

At the beginning of which phase of the cardiac cycle does the second heart sound occur?
  1. A. Atrial systole

  3. C. Rapid ventricular ejection
  4. D. Reduced ventricular ejection
  5. E. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation
  6. F. Rapid ventricular filling
  7. G. Reduced ventricular filling
AnswerE. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation
WhyThe second heart sound is closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves at the end of ejection, which marks the start of isovolumetric relaxation.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E [Chapter 3, V; Figure 3.15]. Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves creates the second heart sound. The closure of these valves corresponds to the end of ventricular ejection and the beginning of ventricular relaxation.

A 64-year old woman with acute myocardial infarction develops a rupture of her papillary muscle anchoring the chordae tendineae of the mitral valve. She becomes short of breath with rales (crackles) on the lung exam. What is the mechanism of the lung finding?
  1. A. Increased right atrial pressure
  2. B. Increased left atrial and hydrostatic capillary pressure
  3. C. Increased compliance of lungs
  4. D. Decreased elasticity of lungs
  5. E. Shunt circulation
AnswerB. Increased left atrial and hydrostatic capillary pressure
WhyA ruptured papillary muscle lets the mitral valve leak, so blood regurgitates into the left atrium, raising left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressure and pushing fluid into the lungs.
ConceptPapillary muscle rupture (acute MR) → ↑ LA and pulmonary capillary pressure → crackles

Q3. An attending presents a case of a patient with aortic stenosis (Increased afterload) and asks you what needs to increase for the ventricle to pump blood into the aorta under these new conditions?
  1. A. Volume
  2. B. Pressure
  3. C. Muscle Mass
  4. D. Preload
AnswerB. Pressure
WhyWith aortic stenosis the LV must generate a much higher systolic pressure to open the narrowed valve and drive blood across it into the aorta.
Explanation from the source
Remember that pressure is always the main driver of blood between any two parts of the body. When LV pressure exceeds Aortic pressure, only then can the aortic valve open and allow blood to pump from the LV to the Aorta. In the case of an increased afterload, the LV now has to pump against a higher pressure and thus needs to build up more pressure to exceed the higher aortic pressure. Though increasing muscle mass is one of the ways the ventricle compensates to produce more pressure, the most direct answer here would be pressure.
ConceptAortic stenosis (↑ afterload): LV must generate more pressure to eject

Q5. A confused medical student decides to come to you and asks why there are two heart sounds if the entire heart contracts simultaneously. What would be the best explanation?
  1. A. The atria and ventricles on the left side contract first, followed by the right
  2. B. The atria and ventricles on the right side contract first, followed by the left
  3. C. The whole heart doesn’t contract simultaneously, ventricles contract first followed by the atria
  4. D. The whole heart doesn’t contract simultaneously, the atria contract first followed by the ventricles
AnswerD. The whole heart doesn’t contract simultaneously, the atria contract first followed by the ventricles
WhyThe heart contracts in sequence, atria then ventricles, and the two sounds are valve closures within ventricular systole: S1 as the AV valves shut at its start and S2 as the semilunar valves shut at its end.
Explanation from the source
Make sure you understand the basics. The atria depolarize and contract first, causing blood to be pushed into the ventricles. The ventricles then depolarize and contract to build-up pressure, eventually pushing blood into the aorta or pulmonary trunk. Both sides of the heart do however contract simultaneously. The two heart sounds S1 (AV valve closure) and S2 (Semilunar valve closure) are proof of this phenomenon.
ConceptWhy there are two heart sounds (keyed: atria contract before ventricles)

Q6: Why do aortic stenosis and regurgitation cause dyspnea?
  1. a. Increased hydrostatic pressure in peripheral capillaries
  2. b. Loss of oncotic pressure
  3. c. Pulmonary hypertension
  4. d. Increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
  5. e. Increased venous return to right heart
AnswerD. d. Increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
WhyAortic stenosis and regurgitation raise LV diastolic and left atrial pressure, which backs up as raised pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, filtering fluid into the lung interstitium and causing dyspnea.
ConceptAortic stenosis/regurgitation → dyspnea via ↑ pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure

  3. C
  4. D

WhyIn anaphylaxis, epinephrine's α1 venoconstriction reverses venous pooling and raises venous return and preload (EDV), so the loop widens to the right with a larger stroke volume.

You gave this patient epinephrine, which is a vasoconstrictor. That peripheral vasoconstriction shoots blood to the heart = increasing Venous Return, which will then increase you’re preload, and subsequently your stroke volume. All seen on this diagram. Choice B was increased contractility. Things that would increase contractility could be drugs such as positive inotropes, like Digoxin(More calcium in heart = greater contraction), or exercise Choice C was increased afterload (ex: patient with hypertension or aortic stiffness).

  3. C
  4. D
  5. No change

Exercise increases heart rate through sympathetic stimulation which subsequently increases contractility and stroke volume.

Point #5 is the end of isovolumetric contraction, so the pressure in the heart is high and it’s ready to pump out the blood(aka systole). Once the pressure in the left ventricle exceeds the pressure of the aortic valve, it will open and proceed into ventricular ejection.

  2. B. Increased afterload

Increased preload. Low right atrial (RA) pressure will increase venous return (VR). RA with lower pressure allows blood to come in easier Low RA → Increased VR → increased end-diastolic volume (point 1, where ventricles completed filling) → increased preload in RV→ more blood going into pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → more blood into LA → more preload in LV. Note: even though the picture on the last slide labels LV, it applies to the right ventricle as well. You don’t need to flow through the heart,can just stop at increased preload in right ventricle. and C. Increased width of the loop = increased SV A = increased preload = increased venous return =increased SV C = increased contractility = increased SV

AV: tricuspid and bicuspid SL: aortic and pulmonary

Chronic pulmonary hypertension results in which of the following? Hint # Law of Laplace P = HT/r P = Pressure H = Height/Thickness T = Tension r = Radius
  1. A. Decreased cardiac work
  2. B. Lowered peripheral arterial blood pressure
  3. C. Right ventricle hypertrophy (Cor Pulmonale)
  4. D. Left ventricle hypertrophy
AnswerC. Right ventricle hypertrophy (Cor Pulmonale)
Explanation from the source
The law of Laplace for a sphere states that the greater the thickness of the wall of the sphere (e.g., right ventricle), the greater the pressure that can be developed. Illustrating this point, the right ventricular wall is thicker than the left ventricular wall because the right ventricle must develop greater pressure to eject blood.
ConceptChronic pulmonary hypertension → right ventricular hypertrophy (cor pulmonale)

A 70 y.o. Man during a visit to his cardiologist is diagnosed with a heart murmur. A chest X-Ray is obtained and reveals an enlarged heart silhouette. Additional test reveal a left sided hypertrophy. In which disorder will left ventricular hypertrophy normally occur?
Show figure
  1. A. Mitral stenosis
  2. B. Aortic stenosis
  3. C. Pulmonary valve regurgitation
  4. D. Tricuspid stenosis
  5. E. Tricuspid regurgitation
AnswerB. Aortic stenosis
WhyAortic stenosis imposes a chronic pressure overload, and by Laplace the LV thickens its wall (concentric hypertrophy) to keep wall tension down while generating higher systolic pressure.
Explanation from the source
L ventricular hypertrophy occurs when the left ventricle has to exert more pressure or accommodate to pump more volume with each stroke. During aortic stenosis the L ventricle has to contract with an increased force, producing a high wall tension so that it can overcome the aortic pressure and expel the blood out of the ventricle. Such increase in pressure can eventually lead to L ventricular hypertrophy.
ConceptValve lesion with ↑ LV pressure/LV hypertrophy = aortic stenosis

A 65-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents with fatigue and dyspnea. Echocardiography shows left ventricular hypertrophy and reduced diastolic filling. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the impaired diastolic filling?
  1. A. Increased afterload due to systemic hypertension
  2. B. Increased myocardial oxygen demand
  3. C. Decreased contractility of the left ventricle
  4. D. Decreased compliance of the left ventricle
  5. E. Increased preload due to fluid retention
AnswerD. Decreased compliance of the left ventricle
WhyHypertrophied myocardium is thick and stiff, so LV compliance falls and a higher filling pressure is needed for the same EDV, impairing diastolic filling.
Explanation from the source
L ventricular hypertrophy leads to decreased compliance of the ventricle. The ventricle becomes stiffer & doesn’t expand efficiently during diastole. As a result, the ventricle can’t fill properly during diastole.
ConceptHypertensive LVH impairs diastolic filling via ↓ LV compliance

Closure of the aortic valve occurs at the onset of which phase of the cardiac cycle?

  4. D. Isovolumetric relaxation
  5. E. Rapid filling
AnswerD. Isovolumetric relaxation
WhyAortic valve closure (S2) seals the ventricle as its pressure falls below aortic pressure, beginning isovolumetric relaxation with both valves shut.
Explanation from the source
The answer is d. (Guyton, pp 99-103.) Closure of the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonic valves) marks the beginning of the isovolumetric relaxation phase of the cardiac cycle. During this brief period (approximately 0.06 s), the ventricles are closed and myocardial relaxation, which began during protodiastole, continues. Intraventricular pressure falls rapidly, although ventricular volume changes little. When intraventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, the mitral and tricuspid valves open and rapid filling of the ventricles begins.

The diagram below illustrates the pressure-volume curves for two different hearts. Which of the following is greater in curve 1?

  2. B. Work
  3. C. Energy consumption
  4. D. Efficiency
  5. E. Stroke volume
AnswerD. Efficiency
WhyBoth loops eject the same SV at the same pressure (equal work), but loop 1 runs at a smaller volume, so by Laplace its wall stress and O₂ use are lower and its efficiency (work/energy) is greater.
Explanation from the source
The answer is d. (Guyton, p 103.) Efficiency is defined as work divided by energy consumption. The heart represented by pressure-volume curve 1 in the diagram has a lower end-diastolic volume and, therefore, ejects blood at a lower wall stress than the heart represented by pressure-volume curve 2. Cardiac energy consumption is directly related to wall stress. Because both hearts eject the same amount of blood (stroke volume) at the same pressure, they perform the same amount of work. Therefore, heart 1 is more efficient because it does the same work using less energy.

When flow through the mitral valve is restricted by mitral stenosis,

WhyIn mitral stenosis exercise raises HR and shortens diastolic filling time, so blood backs up and left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressure spike, causing acute pulmonary edema.
Explanation from the source
The answer is a. (Guyton, pp 247-249.) In patients with mitral stenodecreases sis, the flow of blood from the left atrium to left ventricle during diastole is diminished. The left atrium progressively dilates and left atrial pressure rises. The increase in pressure is transmitted through the pulmonary circulation and eventually leads to an increase in right ventricular pressure. When cardiac output increases during exercise, restriction to flow through the mitral valve causes a sudden increase in pulmonary blood volume, and pulmonary venous and capillary pressures rise, which leads to transudation of fluid into alveoli and pulmonary edema.

Left ventricular wall stress will be decreased by an increase in
  1. A. The left ventricular end-diastolic volume
  2. B. The contractility of the left atrium
  3. C. The thickness of the free wall of the left ventricle
  4. D. The total peripheral resistance
  5. E. The mean arterial blood pressure
AnswerC. The thickness of the free wall of the left ventricle
WhyBy Laplace, wall stress = P × r / wall thickness, so a thicker LV wall (hypertrophy) spreads the load and lowers wall stress.
Explanation from the source
The answer is c. (Berne, 3/e, pp 220-221.) The factors that influence wall stress are given by the Laplace relationship (WS = [P xr] + Th), where P equals the transmural pressure across the wall of the ventricle, r the radius of the ventricle (determined by end-diastolic volume), and Th, the thickness of the ventricular wall. Wall stress is reduced if the wall thickness increases. Increasing the systolic pressure developed by the heart (ventricular transmural pressure) or increasing the end-diastolic volume will increase wall stress. Wall stress will also be increased if total peripheral resistance is increased or mean arterial blood pressure is increased because, under both conditions, the heart will have to develop more pressure.
ConceptLaplace: ↑ LV wall thickness ↓ wall stress

Which one of the following will be observed in a patient with aortic regurgitation?
  1. A. An increased ejection fraction
  2. B. An increased mean blood pressure
  3. C. An increased diastolic blood pressure
  4. D. A decreased pulse pressure
  5. E. A decreased left atrial end-diastolic pressure
AnswerA. An increased ejection fraction
WhyIn aortic regurgitation the backflow enlarges LV filling and the low diastolic aortic pressure eases ejection, so the LV ejects a larger total stroke volume and a higher ejection fraction.
Explanation from the source
The answer is a. (Guyton, pp 154, 246-247.) In aortic regurgitation, some of the blood ejected during systole reenters the left ventricle during diastole. The retrograde flow of blood into the ventricle during diastole increases ventricular volume (preload). At the same time, the retrograde blood flow decreases the diastolic blood pressure. The low diastolic pressure allows the heart to produce a greater ejection fraction. The pulse pressure is widened because of the elevated systolic pressure (brought about by the increased stroke volume) and reduced diastolic pressure (as a consequence of backflow of blood through the incompetent aortic valve).
ConceptAortic regurgitation → ↑ ejection fraction (↑ total SV)

Positive inotropic drugs such a digitalis reduce ischemic cardiac pain (angina) in a dilated failing heart by
  1. A. Decreasing preload
  2. B. Increasing diastolic filling time
  3. C. Decreasing total peripheral resistance
  4. D. Increasing heart rate
  5. E. Increasing coronary blood flow
AnswerA. Decreasing preload
WhyA positive inotrope empties the dilated failing ventricle more completely, lowering end-diastolic volume (preload) and radius, so by Laplace wall tension and myocardial O₂ demand fall.
Explanation from the source
The answer is a. (Guyton, pp 237-238.) Ischemic cardiac pain is proIncreasing coronary blood duced when oxygen demand is greater than the oxygen that can be delivered by the coronary arteries. Positive inotropic agents reduce oxygen flow demand by increasing cardiac contractility. Although under normal circumstances an increase in contractility will increase oxygen demand, in a dilated heart, it actually decreases oxygen demand. The increase in contractility allows the heart to generate adequate force without increasing preload as much. As a result, the volume of the heart is reduced. Reducing volume decreases wall stress, because, according to the law of Laplace, the wall stress is proportional to the product of force and radius (which is proportional to ventricular volume).
ConceptDigitalis relieves angina in dilated failing heart by ↓ preload (smaller ventricle)

Normally, it is pro. . duced by the blood returning to the left atrium from the lungs. AnswerD. 6.25 L/min
Explanation from the source
Central venous pressure: 10 mm Hg Heart rate: 70 beats/min Pulmonary vein2 ] = 0.24 mL O2 /mL Pulmonary artery2 ] = 0.16 mL O2 /mL Whole body O2 consumption: 500 mL/min What is this patient’s cardiac output? Cardiac output is calculated by the Fick principle if whole body oxygen (O2) consumption and in the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein are measured. Mixed venous blood could substitute for a pulmonary artery sample, and peripheral arterial blood could substitute for a pulmonary vein sample. Central venous pressure and heart rate are not needed for this calculation. Cardiac output = (500 mL min) / (0.24 mL O2 mL − 0.16 mL O2 mL) = 6250 mL min or 6.25 L min

Which of the following changes will cause an increase in myocardial O2 consumption?
  1. (A) Decreased aortic pressure
  2. (B) Decreased heart rate
  3. (C) Decreased contractility
  4. (D) Increased size of the heart
  5. (E) Increased influx of Na+ during the upstroke of the action potential
AnswerD. Increased size of the heart
WhyA larger heart has a larger radius, so by Laplace (T = P × r) it must develop more wall tension for the same pressure, raising myocardial O₂ consumption.
Explanation from the source
Myocardial O2 consumption is determined by the amount of tension developed by the heart. It increases when there are increases in aortic pressure (increased afterload), when there is increased heart rate or stroke volume (which increases cardiac output), or when the size (radius) of the heart is increased (T = P × r). Influx of Na+ ions during an action potential is a purely passive process, driven by the electrochemical driving forces on Na+ ions. Of course, maintenance of the inwardly directed Na+ gradient over the long term requires the Na+ −K+ pump, which is energized by adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
Concept↑ Heart size (Laplace: ↑ wall tension) → ↑ myocardial O2 consumption

The mitral valve opens when left atrial pressure becomes higher than left ventricular pressure. This situation occurs when the left ventricular pressure is at its lowest level—when the ventricle is relaxed, blood has been ejected from the previous cycle, and before refilling has occurred.
ConceptMitral valve opens at the end of isovolumetric relaxation

You see a patient in the emergency department with chest pain and history chronic hypertension. His current blood pressure is 170/90. What do you expect to see on EKG and echocardiogram?

  2. B. Left ventricular hypertrophy
  3. C. Right atrial enlargement

WhyChronic systemic hypertension raises LV afterload; the LV thickens its wall to normalize wall tension (Laplace T = P × r ÷ thickness), producing left ventricular hypertrophy.

The answer is d. (Guyton, pp 214, 231.) Cardiac tamponade is a disHypertension order of the heart in which an increase in the volume of pericardial fluid Bra dy cardia Se the Piss = ome! eas filling during diastole. Pulsus paradoxus is a clinical sign in which there is an abnormally large decrease Ventricular dilation (greater than 10 mmHg) in systolic pressure during inspiration.   4. D. I and V
  5. E. I, II, and IV

An 88-year-old female who suddenly stands up after being in the supine position experiences lightheadedness and syncope. Her symptoms can be attributed to which of the following?
  1. A. Increased end diastolic volume
  2. B. Increased venous return
  3. C. Increased capacitance of the veins
  4. D. Increased sympathetic activity
  5. E. Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
AnswerC. Increased capacitance of the veins
WhyOn standing, blood pools in the highly compliant leg veins (venous capacitance), so venous return, preload and cardiac output fall, and cerebral perfusion drops before the baroreflex catches up.
Explanation from the source
[a] No, that would increase pressure. [b] No, decreased [c] The capacitance of the veins allows for large blood volumes to accumulate. [d] Part of Baroreceptor reflex that should activate heart further to counteract drop in pressure [e] Yes, but this is not immediate. | Notes: Syncope = fainting Why d? When a person moves from supine to standing position, blood pools in the veins of the lower extremities. The capacitance of the veins allows for large blood volumes to accumulate. When blood pools in the veins, venous return to the heart decreases and cardiac output decreases (Frank-Starling mechanism), which results in a decrease in mean arterial pressure. Venous pooling also causes increased capillary hydrostatic pressure in the veins of the legs, which results in increased filtration of fluid into the interstitial fluid with a loss of intravascular volume. End-diastolic volume is the amount of blood that is in the ventricles before the heart contracts. Doctors use end-diastolic volume to estimate the heart's preload volume and to calculate stroke volume and ejection fraction. These different measurements indicate the health of a person's heart.
ConceptOrthostatic syncope on standing: ↑ venous capacitance (pooling)

Explanation from the source
Anemia decreases resistance due to several factors: Reduced viscosity due to lower number of circulating RBC’s. When viscosity is lower, blood flows with more ease through the vessels. Systemic vasodilation- the body tries to compensate for the reduced oxygen capacity and delivery to the tissues by promoting vasodilation. This includes the veins as well, which lowers their resistance, this in turn promotes venous return. Increased cardiac output- anemia leads to increased CO to facilitate better oxygen delivery to the tissues. Higher CO means more blood is flowing through the circulation. To accomodate for the increased CO, the body lower venous resistance to let more blood return to the heart in order to maintain the balance between venous return and cardiac output.

Lab results show an elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP). Given his presentation and history, which of the following would best describe the changes in his cardiac and vascular function curves?
Show figure
  1. A) Rightward shift of both the cardiac and vascular function curves due to fluid overload and increased venous return.
  2. B) Leftward shift of the cardiac function curve with no significant change in the vascular function curve due to beta-blocker therapy reducing contractility.
  3. C) Downward rotation of the cardiac function curve with a parallel leftward shift of the vascular function curve due to decreased contractility and hypovolemia.
  4. D) Upward rotation of the cardiac function curve and rightward shift of the vascular function curve due to compensatory mechanisms increasing cardiac output and blood volume.
  5. E) Downward rotation of both the cardiac and vascular function curves due to reduced contractility and decreased preload caused by beta-blockers and lisinopril.
AnswerC) Downward rotation of the cardiac function curve with a parallel leftward shift of the vascular function curve due to decreased contractility and hypovolemia.
WhyReduced contractility (failing heart plus β-blockade) rotates the cardiac function curve downward, and volume loss lowers mean systemic pressure, shifting the vascular function curve left in parallel.
Explanation from the source
C) Downward rotation of the cardiac function curve with a parallel leftward shift of the vascular function curve due to decreased contractility and hypovolemia. Correct: Beta-blocker therapy reduces cardiac contractility, causing the cardiac function curve to rotate downward. The patient’s low blood pressure and potential hypovolemia would shift the vascular function curve leftward due to reduced venous return. Diuretics and fluid management are key. Explanation: In this scenario, the patient presents with heart failure symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue, elevated BNP) alongside hypotension and the use of both carvedilol (a beta-blocker) and lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor). Here's the reasoning for the shifts in the cardiac and vascular function curves: Cardiac function curve: The downward rotation of the cardiac function curve reflects reduced cardiac contractility, a hallmark of heart failure and further exacerbated by the beta-blocker (carvedilol). Carvedilol reduces the heart's ability to contract by blocking beta-receptors, which is beneficial in managing heart failure but lowers cardiac output initially. Vascular function curve: The leftward shift of the vascular function curve reflects a decrease in venous return (or preload). This happens because lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) reduces blood volume by inhibiting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), leading to diuresis and vasodilation. The leftward shift indicates reduced central venous pressure due to this fluid reduction. This combination of decreased contractility and reduced preload explains the downward and leftward shifts in the curves. Why other choices are incorrect: A. Rightward shift of both the cardiac and vascular function curves due to fluid overload and increased venous return: This would apply to cases of fluid overload, not fluid reduction. The ACE inhibitor decreases fluid volume, so a rightward shift of the vascular function curve is incorrect. B. Leftward shift of the cardiac function curve with no significant change in the vascular function curve due to beta-blocker therapy reducing contractility: A beta-blocker reduces cardiac output, but the patient's vascular function curve would shift left due to decreased preload from the ACE inhibitor, which isn't reflected here. D. Upward rotation of the cardiac function curve and rightward shift of the vascular function curve due to compensatory mechanisms increasing cardiac output and blood volume: In this case, cardiac output is reduced, not increased. Compensatory mechanisms like increased preload don't apply here because of ACE inhibitor therapy. E. Downward rotation of both the cardiac and vascular function curves due to reduced contractility and decreased preload caused by beta-blockers and lisinopril: This answer is almost correct, but the vascular function curve would shift leftward, not rotate downward.
ConceptCHF on β-blocker + ACEi: cardiac curve down, vascular curve shifts left

The cardiac function curve rotates downward due to decreased preload. PRBC transfusion restores circulating volume, improving venous return and cardiac output.
